en: Preface to the First Volume of the *Collected Explanations of the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* The Imperial Preface to the Exegetical Commentary on the Sūtra Title, composed for Dharma Master Shi Baoliang of Lingwei Monastery by the Emperor.
Dharma Master Daosheng; Dharma Master Sengliang; Dharma Master Fayao.

The titles and prefaces of the sutras composed by these ten Dharma Masters—Dharma Master Tánjì, Dharma Master Sēngzōng, Dharma Master Bǎoliàng, Dharma Master Zhìxiù, Dharma Master Fǎzhì, Dharma Master Fǎ'ān, and Dharma Master Tánzhǔn—are now recorded in full.
A brief outline of the essential meanings within the preface, categorized into eight sections as follows:

1. Explaining the Title; 2. Discerning the Substance; 3. Narrating Original Existence; 4. Discussing the Transcendence of Names; 5. Explaining the Character "Great" (Mahā-); 6. Interpreting the Character "Sūtra" (Nirvāṇa); 7. Examining the Intent of the Teaching; 8. Determining the Structural Divisions. Preface to the *Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Mingjun records: I have respectfully transcribed this.
For the Emperor’s composition for Dharma Master Bao Liang of Lingwei Monastery: there is no way to convey the ultimate through words, yet words are the very burden of that which is beyond speech.

If words are repeated, one may eventually cease speaking; yet when speech ceases, various views arise in competition. Therefore, the Tathāgata, relying on his original vows, took birth; manifesting the power of compassion, he responded through transformation;

departing from written characters, he established the teachings; and forgetting the marks of the mind, he opened the Way. He sought to distinguish the value of jade from common stone and to separate the waters of the Jing and Wei rivers. He subdued the six masters to rectify the four inversions and turned back the eight heterodoxies to return to the single flavor. He broke the horns of worldly wisdom and silenced the mouths of those with divergent views. He guided those seeking the pearl and opened the days for contemplating the domesticated beast. He rescued those scorched within the burning house and saved those submerged in the surging sea. Thus, when the Dharma rain fell, the parched seeds received nourishment; when the sun of wisdom rose, the long night was granted dawn. He gave voice to Kāśyapa’s pent-up indignation and uttered these words of sincere truth.

Although the two types of giving are presented first and the five great matters are set forth later, the thirty-four questions differ in their specific distinctions; through skillful means of exhortation and guidance, each is answered according to the individual's inclination.
To summarize the essential points of the sutras, they do not go beyond two paths:
Buddha-nature reveals the source from which all things originate;
Nirvana clarifies the ultimate principle toward which all things return.

Neither cause nor effect, neither arising nor acting; its meaning surpasses all myriad virtues, and its reality transcends a hundred negations. Even the "emptiness of emptiness" cannot fathom its true limit, and the "profound mystery" cannot exhaust its wondrous gate. Were it not for one whose virtue equals that of equality and whose mind merges with non-arising, how could one easily enter these golden walls and jade chambers!

There was a śramaṇa named Shi Baoliang from Qingzhou, whose temperament was lofty and refined, and whose spiritual faculties were exceptionally sharp. Having borne rigorous discipline since his youth, he maintained the patience of the Dharma throughout his life; as he grew older, his devotion only deepened, and his vigor did not decline with age. He tirelessly propagated the teachings of the former awakened ones, such that all those of later generations and junior ranks looked up to him in reliance and admiration.

On the eighth day of the fifth month in the eighth year of the Tianjian era, an imperial edict commanded Daolang to compose a commentary on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. It was completed on the twentieth day of the ninth month. Illuminating the subtle words and extolling the True Path, the interlocking chains were unraveled and the net of doubt was cleared away; as the various points and their logical flow became clear and complete, they may now be briefly described.
Although I have been occupied with state affairs, I intend to peruse this work.
I shall briefly write these few lines as a preface and record.
According to Daosheng:
Now, the ultimate truth is spontaneous, and awakening is its dark resonance;
since truth is without deviation, how could awakening be easy?
This unchanging essence is a profound and constant illumination; it is only through delusion that we stray from it, for the reality has never been something external to us.
If one can seek through inquiry, one will turn back from delusion and return to the ultimate; returning to the ultimate, one attains the source.
This appears as if it were beginning anew, yet what begins must necessarily end.
One is constantly obscured by this, but if one traces its course, it is simply that I have now realized what was already there; it is not something newly manifested in the present.
If there were nothing existing outside of the present, then nothing could be considered "Great" from the outset.
Since it is called "Great," it is therefore "Constant.
Being constant necessarily entails the extinction of all burdens; this is what is further termed *parinirvāṇa*.
"Parinirvāṇa," correctly translated, means "extinction.
Yet, when its meaning and etymology are considered, there are many different interpretations.
Now, this sutra clarifies the eternal, so as to cause those who are deluded to submit.
Once their delusions are forever subdued, they subsequently attain awakening.
When awakened, all delusions are extinguished; to attribute [this state] to a name, is it not simply "the Ever-Spoken"?
Furthermore, for a Bodhisattva who dwells in this sutra, all afflictions have already been subdued and extinguished.
Although they have not yet reached the ultimate, they are able to manifest *parinirvāṇa*.
Among all manifestations, there is no "wondrous" *nirvāṇa*; furthermore, to manifest nothing at all is what constitutes the Great.
To further employ this title for the sutra is surely to doubly extol its perfection and excellence.
According to Sengliang:
"This is the ultimate designation for the Tathāgata’s divine way and the comprehensive name for the eight flavors of permanence and bliss.

*Nirvāṇa* is a term that differs from the vernacular; just as there are dialects such as those of Chu and Xia, these terms appear interchangeably before and after, resulting in three names: *niyuan*, *niepan*, and *niyu*."
The term "Nirvāṇa" is the phonetic transcription from Central India;
it contains manifold meanings, none of which have a single corresponding name in this land [of China], so its foreign original has been preserved as is.
"Parinirvāṇa" is said to mean "not," and it is also called "non-existence.
"Nirvāṇa" refers to birth, cessation, cause, and characteristics.
Birth is the root of the eight sufferings; since the Buddha is devoid of these, he does not undergo birth.
Its lifespan is equal in measure to the great void; it is not extinguished.
It is not obtained through the cause of conditioned action; therefore, it is without cause.
Its essence lacks the ten marks; it is markless.
The dharmas of the stage of no-more-learning constitute its entire essence; briefly stated, it is characterized by three aspects to signify the path of the spirit:
first, prajñā; second, the dharmakāya; and third, liberation.

When discussing prajñā, the achievement of the three types of supernormal knowledge becomes manifest; when expounding upon the dharma-body, the principle of responsive transformation is identical; and when speaking of liberation, it is therein that all virtues are fully perfected.
To speak of these three dharmas is sufficient to clarify the ultimate of the divine way (*śendao*).
As for "Great," it clarifies its constancy; furthermore, it is because of Great Self, Great Bliss, and Great Purity, which will be explained later.

From the site of enlightenment until his final passing between the twin trees, the Tathāgata preached the Nirvāṇa three times in total; two of these were expedient means and one was the ultimate truth.
The first instance, which opened up the three ultimate vehicles, was an expedient means wherein he spoke only of liberation as Nirvāṇa, while regarding both body and wisdom as conditioned phenomena.

Within the two types of skillful means, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* teaches that the three [vehicles] are ultimately destroyed; yet because [the Buddha] still possesses a body and wisdom, this is merely conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Now, the teaching at the twin trees—that body and wisdom are themselves nirvāṇa—is the teaching of ultimate, remainderless [nirvāṇa].
"Sūtra" is the Hu (Central Asian) pronunciation for *sūtra*; the term *sūtra* contains five meanings.
According to Fa-yao:
"Now, Nirvāṇa is the ultimate convergence of the primal source and the great final destination when all numerical calculations have been exhausted."

As for its essence, it is wondrously transcendent beyond the realm of existence and non-existence, and profoundly surpasses the distinctions of names and categories; words cannot exhaust it, and designations cannot reach its limit.
However, since there is nothing that can match the Ultimate, we rely on designations to approximate it;
and since there is nothing that can reveal Reality, we rely on words to manifest it.

As for its names, none are greater than this in their totality; thus, it is said to encompass all principles and its title crowns all meanings—therefore, within a single name, there are immeasurable names.

Thus, the sounds of the original tongue have no means to translate its designations, and the language of Jin has no way to substitute for its titles. Therefore, those who wish to match these sounds with their equivalents miss the essential meaning, and those who pair these names with their counterparts deviate from the intended purpose. This is because even the ultimate expressions of that which possesses a name cannot fully exhaust it; how much less so can this apply to that which is beyond naming?

Therefore, the supreme title of Nirvana encompasses such vast and profound meaning that, were one to analyze and discern it, the discussion would be inexhaustible; how could it be limited merely to the three [perfections] such as Prajñā to reach its ultimate consummation?
To briefly set forth the essentials, one enters Nirvana by way of these three names.
Thus, the analogy of the letter "I" (the trident) is indeed appropriate.
Consequently, these three are distinct in name but identical in substance; they do not differ in essence.
If their essence were distinct, then nirvana would be identical to those dharmas that are conventionally designated as being produced by causes;
being empty and not real, how could it be called "eternal and blissful"?
According to Tánjì:
Now, the Great Nirvāṇa is the ultimate designation for the numinous Way of the Great Sage and the collective name for the eight flavors [of liberation].
This is the final teaching of the Path, expressed through liberated speech and diverse pronouncements; therefore, its designations are not uniform.

When rendered into the sounds of India, the meaning is so comprehensive that no single word exists here in this land to correspond to it; thus, while its meanings are manifold—being called "unborn," and also "unextinguished," "unconditioned," and "signless"—it remains one in essence.
The reason it is called "non-arising" is that it has forever severed the four modes of birth.
The reason it is called "non-extinction" is that its measure is equal to the great void; therefore, it is termed non-extinction.
That which is called "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta) is so called because it is not produced by the processes of arising and ceasing; therefore, it is called unconditioned.
That which is called "signless" (animitta) is so called because its essence is utterly free from the ten signs; therefore, it is called signless.
Regarding *nirvāṇa*, all the merits of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣabhūmi*) constitute its essence; herein, three matters are briefly cited to illustrate it.
These three matters are: *prajñā* (wisdom), *dharmakāya* (dharma-body), and *vimukti* (liberation).
Speaking of prajñā, its clear wisdom pervades all objects;
distinguishing the dharmakāya, its clarity is fully equipped to respond to all forms;
designating liberation, it clarifies that the manifold afflictions do not arise.
Because wisdom pervades all objects, the merit of the three types of penetration is manifest;
because it fully responds to all forms, it can respond simultaneously to diverse regions;
and because no manifold afflictions arise, the enlightened spirit is seen to encompass all, thereby achieving perfection.
Regarding the term "Great," it is because it contains the Great Self (mahātman). As the subsequent text states: "For example, there is a secret formula that encompasses all formulas;
this sutra is likewise, for it contains much within its embrace."
The reason for this is that from the Deer Park until the Twin Trees, there have been three explanations of *nirvāṇa*:
first, it was clarified at the initial Deer Park that the three vehicles each possess their own distinct *nirvāṇa*;
second, it was clarified that the three vehicles share a single *nirvāṇa*.
The true teaching of the Threefold Knowledge (trividyā) subverts the two provisional means, declaring that the body and wisdom are themselves nirvāṇa.
For this reason, it contains much within it and is therefore called "Great" (mahā).
As for "Sūtra," the word in the language of the Hu is *sūtra*, which contains five meanings:
First, that which can give birth; second, subtle emergence; third, a surging spring; fourth, a plumb line; fifth, a flower garland.
Sometimes the text is taken as the sūtra, sometimes the principle is taken as the sūtra, or sometimes the entire forty fascicles of text constitute the essence of the sūtra.
The reason it is said that "it can produce" is that when the practitioner seeks this text, it is able to produce roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
The reason it is said that "it arises subtly" is that the roots of goodness gradually increase.
Just as one first takes the three refuges and next observes the five precepts, and so on until the attainment of the Way, there is thus the meaning of "subtle arousal.
As for the term "gushing spring," it is used as a metaphor for how the text expresses the underlying principle; because it is inexhaustible, it is like a spring.

The reason for speaking of "plumb lines and carpenter’s squares" is that the plumb line is fundamentally used to distinguish the curvature and straightness of wood; it is clear that this scripture distinguishes the principles of the heterodox and the orthodox, which can be understood by relying on the text, and thus it is known as the "plumb line and square."
Therefore, it is called "stringing together" (granthi-mālā): flowers scattered upon the ground are not used by people;
only when they are strung together with thread do they become head-ornaments for people.
If they are not strung with thread, they are not used by people.
If clarity does not employ literary expression to discern the principles, it is of no use to people;
because employing literary expression to discern the principles is of use to people, it is like a thread.
Although this meaning exists, what is now called "sūtra" (經) is one of these five meanings, possessing the sense of being a "binding garland."
According to Sengzong, this is the ultimate designation for the exhaustion of all afflictions and the supreme appellation for the myriad virtues.
As for "Great," it has two meanings: first, the greatness of the teaching; second, the greatness of the principle.

Why is this so? From its beginning at the Deer Park until its conclusion at the Lotus Sūtra, [the previous teachings] did not fully distinguish cause and effect nor exhaustively clarify the objects of cognition and practice;
therefore, they are termed "Small. This teaching is perfect and complete, and is thus called "Great."
In the past, the nirvana of the three vehicles was not the true ultimate; it was the "small" within the realm of principle.
Now, it is clarified that the Dharmakāya-prajñā exists beyond all worldly burdens; this is the "great" within the realm of principle, which is why it is called "Great."
*Nirvāṇa* is the correct phonetic transcription from India; in this [Chinese] language it is called "liberation" (*mukti*), meaning to be freed from the myriad burdens.
Once these burdens and afflictions have ceased, one’s essence is endowed with all virtues. To state them briefly, there are three which can encompass all others:
first, the *dharmakāya*; second, *prajñā*; and third, liberation.
The wondrous existence is pure, its essence being nothing other than the Dharma; therefore, it is called "Dharma.
The wondrous essence is distinct and separate from the great void; therefore, it is called "body" (kāya).
The spirit is clarified and shines vacuously, its discernment reaching everywhere; therefore, it is called *prajñā*.
The Way stands high above the myriad delusions, its essence free from defilement and entanglement; therefore, it is termed *vimukti*.
These three virtues are identical in essence but distinct in meaning.
Although there are three designations for the meaning within a single essence, the reason why only liberation (*vimukti*) is selected here to title this scripture is due to three points:
first, to clarify that the principle lies beyond all delusions.
Second is the refutation of the former understanding of liberation. Why?
Because in the past, followers of the Lesser Vehicle were troubled by the arousal of body and cognition; they sought to extinguish this affliction, relying their sentiments upon liberation.
Because the physical body and wisdom have both come to an end, this is a solitary liberation; therefore, it is known as "small.
What is clarified today possesses all virtues in its essence, wears the Prajñā of the Dharmakāya, and exists eternally; therefore, it is called "great."
"Sūtra" refers to the fact that the Buddhas of the three periods of time, from the stage of ordinary beings to that of the sages, have all passed through this.

According to Baoliang: "The Supreme Spirit is profound and tranquil; its essence transcends both existence and non-existence. Its concentrated illumination is empty and still, and its subtlety exceeds the realm of numbers. Its purport lies beyond birth and death and transcends conditioned phenomena within the sphere of language. Therefore, the Great Awakened One bestowed his compassion, taking the alleviation of suffering as the foundation. Yet, because the faculties of sentient beings differ, the teachings are divided into five distinct categories."

Just as sentient beings are obscured by heavy delusions and have not yet been able to rest in the profound, the teaching of expedient means was first opened up to support the present principle of perfect permanence.

Once sentient beings have received the former teachings to cultivate their minds, they can then slightly penetrate the void to enter the Way, realizing both the wheel of permanence and the wheel of impermanence simultaneously; they discern that birth and death are the existence of non-existence, and nirvana is the non-existence of non-existence.

Having already established oneself in the truth and awakened to the principle, and having recognized suffering and emptiness to sever delusion—if one does not personally practice to enter the Way and give rise to the knowledge that conditions the realization of the principle, then afflictions and delusions will not be dispelled, and birth-and-death will be difficult to eliminate.
Therefore, the rise of the present teaching reveals the wondrous essence of the divine spirit.
It distinguishes birth and death, taking the two types of suffering as its foundation;
it clarifies nirvana, taking permanence and bliss as its source.
The wondrous substance is eternally unmoving, while its function constantly changes yet remains indestructible; it is without name and without form, beyond the distinctions of the hundred negations.

Now, the term "Nirvana" is applied according to this function; it is the general name for the supramundane dharma, the universal designation that encompasses all virtues, the essential heading that replaces birth and death, and the supreme teaching of the state where nothing remains.

When obstructions and karmic burdens are exhausted, the myriad practices return to the truth; with no virtue left unfulfilled and all functions complete, the causal stage transforms into the fruit, which is named Great Nirvana.
Therefore, the text below states: "If even a single virtue is not cultivated, then one cannot be called 'Great Nirvāṇa'.
However, these words are merely the local dialect of that region.

Since the Sage originated from that country, there is no name here [in China] that can serve as a direct translation; rather, within the texts, he is merely explained through analogies and defined according to his essential meaning.
Nevertheless, his virtues are profound and vast, making them difficult to enumerate exhaustively; for now, I shall briefly set forth their essential points.
The principle may be threefold; thus, the "Chapter on Sorrowful Lamentation" clarifies this, referring to the Precious City of the True Dharma and the Secret Treasury.
What is the meaning of these two: first, the designation of distinct virtues, and second, the reliance upon functional efficacy?

Now, Nirvana has no substantial body; it is accomplished through the accumulation of manifold virtues. Therefore, the metaphor of a jeweled city is employed to illustrate this principle; it is not something to be clung to by those of the Two Vehicles, for they regard it as mere rubble rather than a treasure.
Since its essence already encompasses all perfections, what treasure could possibly be lacking?

It is simply that the former teachings were not yet clear, whereas the present exposition has now begun to manifest them. To conceal the reality and reveal the provisional—how could this be anything other than "esoteric"?

Second, regarding the citation of specific virtues, the "Chapter on Merits" states: "That is to say, the Great, the Constant, the Great Self, the Great Bliss, and Purity," and so forth. These are the supreme causes for achieving nirvana; therefore, they are cited individually to highlight their excellence.

Because its essence is without arising or ceasing, it is called "Eternal"; because its eight functions are sovereign, it is termed "Self"; because it is tranquil and free from suffering, it is designated as "Bliss"; because defilements are forever exhausted, it is named "Pure"; and because its essential form is boundless, it is called "Great. These are merely words of praise and laudatory epithets.
Thus, praising its craftsmanship and utility, the "Lion’s Roar" chapter refers to it as "taking refuge in an island.

It enables sentient beings to escape suffering and abide in eternal peace, to leave the river and ascend to the island, crossing the deep ocean of the four flows to reach the shore of non-action (asaṃskṛta).

If one seeks its name, it employs the principle of numbers to transcend words; thus, the Sage’s transformation is extensively bestowed, and his virtues are discussed in myriad ways. Therefore, at the very beginning of establishing the school, he borrowed the metaphor of the letter *i*, saying that its three dots are neither vertical nor horizontal, thereby differing from the former explanations of "having a remainder" or "lacking virtue," and clarifying the possession of the Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Vimukti.

However, these three are essential elements at the culmination of the path of transformation; they further penetrate all virtues, distinguish the form and mind within causal conditions, and manifest the supreme function of the Buddha-fruit, wherein there is no stimulus that goes unanswered—thus it is called the Dharma-body.
The clarity of all objects of perception is called *prajñā* (wisdom).
That this very essence is free from all burdens is termed *vimokṣa* (liberation).
One must understand that while each individual virtue is not itself *nirvāṇa*, their collective totality constitutes its essence.
Therefore, in the following "Chapter on the Merits of Names," the eight flavors of sweet ghee are used as a metaphor for this praise.

When discussing the ultimate and conventional truths, their two natures are fundamentally identical and their functions do not conflict; yet, when darkness departs and the conventional is exhausted, falsehood recedes and the ultimate is revealed, shining forth with brilliant and penetrating clarity—thus one is called a Buddha.

Since this sutra unfolds the teachings for transcending the world within the midst of supramundane dharmas, serving as a proximate support for external ordinary beings and the essential path for those of inferior capacity, its principle is perfect and benefits others; its essence is non-action, yet it promotes virtue.
However, the text is extensive and its meaning profound; thus, it is entrusted to later commentators for exposition.
As for the term "sūtra" (jīng), it takes "passing through" (jīngyóu) as its primary sense.

For any student, if one does not rely on these principles and teachings, there is no way to attain understanding; therefore, the single character "sūtra" permeates the literary and logical structure of this entire work.
According to Zhixiu:
"This is essentially the general designation for the ultimate, perfected virtue.
If one were to provide the full title according to the old texts, it should be rendered as *Mahāparinirvāṇa*."
Now, the Way transcends all that is erroneous, yet its principle returns to a single unity.
Because it returns to a single unity, consciousness is thereby perfected;
because it transcends all that is erroneous, no words can reach its ultimate limit.
However, since names are perceived through their traces, one may also seek out the names to know the source.
Yet, as for the emergence of these names and traces, they originated in India;
in our Great Liang, it was likewise appropriate that there should be a corresponding designation.
Now that the proximity of the propagation of the Way has already been manifested in the Western Regions, it remains unmeasured how it was translated in this land.

Therefore, both former sages and later philosophers have all followed the established texts, describing them without creating new ones; thus, the title is placed at the beginning of the scripture, embodying its virtue and name.
Now, names are used to designate essences; because there is an essence, there are virtues.
The essence is the fundamental source of the perfect, wondrous existence; the virtues are the flowing currents of *prajñā* and liberation.
When discussing their virtues, they appear manifold; when examining their essence, they are but one.
Although their names differ, in reality there is no distinction. Why is this so?

The essence of ultimate perfection possesses the significance of being a standard for emulation, and is thus called the Dharma-body; it possesses the function of tranquil illumination, and is designated as Prajñā; it possesses the virtue of being free from all burdens, and is termed Liberation.

This is precisely because the essence of liberation is that which can illuminate, and the essence of that which can illuminate is liberation; there is no separate essence, yet it possesses manifold virtues. Therefore, the general name "Nirvana" is used as its title.
The "perfect essence" (yuan ti) is termed "total," for because its essence is perfect, it fully encompasses all meanings.

In the subsequent scripture, the "Chapter on the Merits of Names and Titles," the name is explained through these various meanings as follows: "Endowed with eight flavors, it is called Great Nirvana. The eight flavors are: first, permanence; second, constancy; third, peace; fourth, coolness; fifth, non-aging; sixth, non-death; seventh, stainlessness; and eighth, bliss."

Upon examining the intent behind the teachings of this sutra, from the Tathāgata’s initial transformation of beings at the Deer Park to the ultimate realization of his purpose at Vulture Peak, it is clear that he only elucidated the extremity of the Way—the exhaustion of all traces—and that goodness inevitably leads to Bodhi. He did not yet distinguish how all sentient beings, possessing emotion and vital breath, could all achieve the Peerless State; he merely spoke of the longevity of the Buddha’s lifespan as being many times greater than previously stated, but did not clarify that the Perfect Enlightenment is empty, tranquil, profound, and indestructible.

This present sutra takes the ultimate, wondrous conditioned phenomena as its guiding manual and the eternally abiding Buddha-nature as its central tenet. It clarifies that for icchantikas, the true cause remains unaltered; it distinguishes the Dharma-body as the manifest and majestic perfect fruit. This is what is called the supreme teaching of no remainder and the ultimate, final discourse.
"Sūtra" means "that which is traversed.
In India, texts that elucidate principles are collectively termed *sūtra*.
The term *sūtra* encompasses a multitude of meanings.
Why is this? It is like the flow of a spring, a subtle emergence, a gushing fountain, or a plumb line;
as for the meaning of "passing through," it is merely one aspect thereof.
However, the bibliographic records of the Liang dynasty all categorized works by their titles as "Jing" (Scriptures).

Therefore, scholars of broad perspective have simplified the complex and adopted brevity, citing them by their essential titles; thus, they do not deviate from the singular principle of comprehensive inclusion, while also conforming to custom to achieve conciseness.
According to the *Fazhi*:
"Now, words and images arise from within the realm of numbers; forms and names emerge from amidst the burdens of existence.
Since the divine way of the Perfected One is devoid of both image and word, how could it further possess any forms or names?"
Perfect Way cannot be designated by a single term; therefore, it is given the general name based on its encompassing virtues, which is forcibly called "Nirvana.
This is an Indic sound; to preserve the foreign name in its entirety, one should say "Parinirvāṇa."
In foreign lands, this name has many meanings; since there is no corresponding sound in these lands to translate it back, we have retained the foreign term as its name.
Now, since the name is merely provisional, does that name itself not also rely on words? To express the principle through words is likewise a provisional expression of words.
If it may be expressed through words, I beg you to attempt to speak of it.
Taking *nirvāṇa* as the ultimate principle, it transcends the realm of calculation and notation and lies beyond the traces of the profound darkness.
When speaking of its subtle penetration, this resides in that which is inherently existent (*bennyou*).

What is called "originally existing" (benyou) is an esoteric indication that [the fruit] exists across future, separated lifetimes; it does not mean that it exists within the present, contemporary lifetime.

If one takes the future as being existent, then for those who receive consciousness, the source and root already exist of themselves even before causes have been created; therefore, it is said to be "originally existing."
If it existed inherently from the outset before the causes were produced, then it would not depend on karmic conditions to initiate its beginning; therefore, it is not something newly created.
Since it is not newly created, it is described as being "in the future."
The three periods of time are not identical; they must await the creation of karma before they can be said to exist.

Although [the nature] exists inherently from the beginning, because that which is yet to come has not yet arisen and that which has already passed no longer functions, a revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*) is required.

However, as one now intends to manifest that the essence of its fruit is perfectly complete and fulfilled, a name is assigned to it; thus, the meaning of the "ten thousand virtues" is none other than the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, by first opening the letter "I," the three virtues are employed to clarify *nirvāṇa*, thereby distinguishing it from previous teachings.

Why is this? In former teachings, body and wisdom were considered conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); as they were not yet liberated from the bonds of the fruit, one had to extinguish body and wisdom for them to become unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, those extinguished phenomena were described as unconditioned liberation.

If this dharma of cessation can be described by such meanings as liberation, nirvāṇa, the unconditioned, bliss, and purity, it is therefore spoken of in contrast to birth-and-death as *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder).
Thus, although the Nirvana previously taught also possessed multiple meanings, it simply could not speak of the body and wisdom, which is why those three elements were all absent.
Now that there exists this ultimate teaching, which differs from the former, one must maintain the three virtues; that is, taking the very body and wisdom as liberation.

Regarding "preserving the three virtues" (*triguṇa*): this reveals that the single essence of the three virtues constitutes the dharma of *nirvāṇa*; the meaning of *nirvāṇa* is that all dharmas possess these virtues.
As for the essence of the three virtues being the dharma of *nirvāṇa*, the Sūtra states, "Dharma is called its own essence"; therefore, the essence itself is taken as the dharma.

Regarding the three virtues as the meaning of *nirvāṇa*: because the three virtues reside within the Dharma, the Dharma possesses these three meanings; therefore, the meaning of each of the three virtues constitutes the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the statement that the *dharmakāya* signifies the meaning of *nirvāṇa*: "Dharma" takes the principle as its function, while "body" (*kāya*) is a synonym for essence.
It is precisely because this essence can be taken as a model (*dharma*) that it is called the *dharmakāya*.
Since eternal nirvāṇa now possesses a substantial essence that can be taken as a model, the meaning of the *dharmakāya* is established as the meaning of nirvāṇa.

As for the meaning of *prajñā* being the meaning of nirvāṇa: *prajñā* functions through the power of discerning insight; since eternal nirvāṇa is said to possess a substantial essence, it is characterized by non-knowing yet not not knowing—this is precisely *prajñā*. Therefore, the meaning of *prajñā* is established as the meaning of nirvāṇa.

Regarding the statement that "the meaning of liberation is the meaning of nirvāṇa": liberation takes the sense of being freed from bondage as its meaning. Although the essence of one who abides eternally in nirvāṇa remains present, they are liberated from both the bondage of causes and the bondage of effects; therefore, the meaning of liberation is taken as the meaning of nirvāṇa.
Previously, when discussing *nirvāṇa*, it was stated that both body and wisdom are utterly extinguished; therefore, both are clearly explained here.
As for the other meanings, they are common to both teachings and are identical in substance to liberation; thus, they are omitted and not analyzed further.
The merit of my doctrine lies in its realization by the Awakened One; Nirvana is the Treasure of the Dharma. Since the person and the Dharma are distinct, there is no need for further explanation.
If all meanings of the myriad virtues were simply the meaning of Nirvana, then the Dharma would be the Perfect Dharma and its name would likewise be the Perfect Name.
When both name and reality are perfected, one reaches the ultimate pinnacle of the Way of the Divine Person; therefore, it is named Nirvana.
Furthermore, the repetition of the term "great" serves to manifest that both its name and its principle have reached the absolute extreme.
In the past, the extinction of these two matters was not yet what made it "Great";

now, with the clarification of Nirvana, its essence is perfect and complete. Since the principle accords with the name and the name does not deviate from the principle, both name and principle reach their ultimate limit—only then is it truly "Great."

As for the term "sūtra," it is only that which is uttered from the golden mouth [of the Buddha] and whose principles are thus established that may be called a sūtra; those composed by disciples, unless authorized by the Buddha, cannot be so called.
What is this? Briefly, there are two meanings for the etymological definition of the word "sūtra":
first, it is defined as meaning "constant."
Regarding the second point, "the words are eternal":
Now, the Perfect Man speaks only after his wisdom has reached its ultimate limit; thus, his words necessarily accord with principle.
Since none of the sages can alter these words, they are called eternal.
From the transcendence of the mundane to the entry into the sacred, there is nothing that does not proceed by means of these two.
Since the Buddha’s teachings have fully exhausted these two principles, they are entitled to be called *sūtras*.

As for what I, your disciple, have spoken, my reasoning has not yet been fully discerned and my words have not yet reached the truth; since I have not yet reached the ultimate limit regarding these two constant principles, it cannot be called a *sūtra*.
Therefore, although Vimalakīrti and Śrīmālā had things to say, they required the Buddha’s seal of approval before their words could be designated as sūtras.
According to Fǎ'ān: "The designation 'Nirvāṇa' refers to the ultimate fruit."

This ultimate fruition transcends form and sound, excelling all that can be conveyed through words; it casts off all burdens and is endowed with every virtue. Thus, it is able to transcend birth and extinction, remaining eternally present and immutable.
Why is this so? For when the illumination of the Dharma is not yet exhaustive, new knowledge shifts one’s spirit.
Since delusion and entanglement serve as its causes, that which arises must inevitably pass away.
Now, this ultimate fruit is in essence free from even a speck of dust; produced by the illumination of its causes, it stands majestic and eternal—is this not fitting?
To draw forth sentient beings, it is described through the metaphor of the three virtues:
because its sole substance is the Dharma, it is called the Dharmakāya.
When the afflictions of delusion have perished, it is called liberation;
when that which is illumined leaves nothing behind, it is termed prajñā.
The single name "Dharmakāya" designates its wondrous essence.
The two titles, "Wisdom" (Jñāna) and "Cessation" (Prahāṇa), are cited to highlight its preeminent virtues.
To speak briefly of these three [aspects], they already encompass all its manifold excellences.

The single name used in India combines these three meanings; since a single Chinese term could not exhaust its full significance, the original Indic sound was retained to serve as the title at the beginning of the sutra.

As for the "Great" (Mahā): the name "Nirvāṇa" is a general designation encompassing manifold meanings; since this title was already applied even when one had not yet fulfilled the causal stage (*hetubhūmi*), the prefix "Great" has been added so that the essential purport may be made clearly manifest.
According to Tan Zhun:
"This is, indeed, the numinous abode of auspiciousness and the empty chamber where purity arises.

Examining its causes, its practice surpasses the ten stages; scrutinizing its fruit, its subtlety reaches the ultimate beginning. It cannot be altered by dark creation, nor can it be moved by mysterious operation; it is profoundly divine in its singular stillness—this takes 'permanence' as its fundamental principle."
However, its manifold excellences cannot be fully expressed in words; therefore, I shall briefly attribute three virtues to it:
taking its profound illumination and empty clarity, I name it Prajñā (Wisdom);
taking its responsive yet unmoving stillness, I call it Dharmakāya (Dharma-body).
When the fetters and delusions have entirely vanished, it is called liberation (*vimukti*).
Since these three meanings are thus clarified, the name "Nirvana" is established.

"Da" (Great) is a term from the Liang region, while "Nirvana" is a common word in the Western Regions. Because that term contains many layers of meaning, there is no way to translate it partially here; therefore, the original foreign title is retained as the heading.
Preface to the Scripture Title (I): Highlighting the Essential Points within the Preface.
Regarding the eight examples on the right, first is the "Explanation of Names" (*Shiming*). According to the preface by Sengliang: [The text continues with the specific details of the commentary.]

The ultimate designation for the Tathāgata’s divine path and the collective name for the eight flavors of eternal bliss are these unconventional terms, which differ according to regional dialects like those of Chu and Xia: namely, *nirvāṇa*, *niyuan*, and *niyu*.
"Nirvāṇa" is the Middle Indic pronunciation; its name encompasses manifold meanings, and there is no corresponding term in this land [of China] by which it may be translated.
Fayao, Tanji, Baoliang, Tana'i, Zhixiu, Fazhi, Fa'an, and Tanzhun all agree on this point.
However, what Fayao describes differs slightly, stating:
"Therefore it is said that within a single name there are immeasurable names.
Examining this statement, it follows that the name 'Nirvana' not only contains a multitude of meanings, but also contains a multitude of names.
Furthermore, Bao Liang said:

"Although both cases likewise lack a translation, one does not say that 'the name contains manifold meanings'; rather, it is said that 'it is explained by way of analogy' (*xunkuang*) to indicate the interpretation of the meaning.
The Preface states:

Since the Sage has already departed from that [land], there is no way to provide a direct translation here; one can only explain the meaning by means of glosses, analogies, and indications within the text.
Fa’an also said: "A gloss (xùn) brings forth the various meanings."
Daosheng said: "The term 'extinction' (nirodha) is used to designate the name; yet, if one takes its meaning and interpretation, there are naturally many other aspects.
Now, this sutra clarifies the eternal, so as to cause those who are deluded to submit."
Once that delusion is forever subdued, one subsequently attains awakening.
When awakening occurs, all delusions are extinguished; to give this its name, it is surely what is called "the constant preaching.

Furthermore, for a Bodhisattva who dwells in this sutra, all afflictions have already been subdued and extinguished; although they have not yet reached the ultimate limit, they are able to manifest parinirvāṇa.

The multitude is shown that there is no "sublime" nirvana; furthermore, taking the non-indication of anything as its greatness, this scripture is further extolled by this title—this is surely to doubly praise it as being utterly perfect.
Huilang recounted Fayao’s words, saying:
"This term 'quiescent extinction' (nirvāṇa) refers to the name for the fact that the mind and consciousness are unattainable.
He further recounted Tanxian’s words, saying:
Sengzong said: "These words signify freedom from entanglement;
these words signify liberation."
Seeking "non-entanglement" and "liberation," their names differ while their meaning is one; thus, they both refer to being free from bondage.
Nevertheless, both "liberation" (jie) and "freedom" (tuō) are names for virtuous qualities.
The designation "unencumbered" (wulei) encompasses all that is to be abandoned.

According to Sengzhao’s *Treatise*, this term "extinction" (mièdù) is also called "non-action" (wéiwéi); it refers to the extinction of birth and death and the crossing to the other shore—the state of profound stillness.
Huiji of Kuaiji agreed with him, saying:
"This refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Zhizang and Fayun also agreed with him, saying:
Regarding this term "nirodha" (extinction):

according to Mingjun’s examination, although there is no direct translation for it, it is not the collective name for all virtues; rather, it is the general designation for the state of being free from all burdens.
Why is this? The following passage states: "Parinirvāṇa: 'pari' means non-existence, and also means absence;
'nirvāṇa' means birth, and also means cessation."
Thus, the names of the "Non-entanglements" (wulei) are fully enumerated here as an explanatory commentary.
2. Discerning the Essence (biantie), Part Two. According to Dao Sheng:
Now, the True Principle is spontaneous; awakening is likewise a dark resonance with it.
Truth is without differentiation; how could awakening be easy?
This unchanging essence is a state of profound, constant illumination; it is only through delusion that one deviates from it, though the reality has never been something external to me.
If one can seek through this, one will immediately turn back from delusion and return to the ultimate.
Master Sengliang states:
"The dharmas of the stage of no-more-learning are all its essence."
The Buddha briefly expounded three [aspects] to characterize the divine path:
first, *prajñā* (wisdom); second, the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body); and third, liberation (*vimukti*). Fayao records:
The title "Nirvāṇa" is profoundly extensive in its meaning; how could it be exhausted merely by the three [perfections] such as Prajñā, which only briefly cite its essentials?
Thus, these three differ in name but are identical in reality; they do not possess distinct essences.
If their substance were distinct, then, like all phenomena established through causes as mere provisional names, they would be empty and unreal; how then could they be called "permanent"?
Master Sengzong’s preface states:
"Once the accumulated afflictions have ceased, the substance is replete with manifold virtues. To briefly cite three of these, they are sufficient to encompass all others."
However, these three virtues are one in essence yet distinct in meaning; there are three designations for their meanings based upon a single substance.
Bao Liang’s preface states:

"When obstructions and defilements are exhausted and the myriad practices return to the truth, no virtue remains unfulfilled and all functions are sufficient. Transforming the causal stage into the fruit, it is named Great Nirvana."
However, his virtue is profound and vast, making it difficult to enumerate exhaustively; I shall briefly set forth its essentials, which may be summarized in three principles:
first, the Precious City of the True Dharma; second, the designation of distinct virtues; and third, the application of skillful means.
Why is this? Now, Nirvana has no intrinsic substance; it is accomplished through the accumulation of manifold virtues. To illustrate this principle, the metaphor of a precious city is employed.
As for these distinct virtues, they refer to the Great Permanence, the Great Self, and so forth; these are the supreme causes that bring about Nirvana.
As for "utility," it refers to taking refuge in the island-continent, which enables sentient beings to escape suffering and attain peace.
Zhi Xiu’s preface states:
"The essence is the fundamental source of the perfect, ultimate, and wondrous existence."
Virtue is the outflow of prajñā, the dharma-body, and liberation.
Although virtues may be manifold when discussed, their essence is one when analyzed. Why is this so?
That which is perfectly consummate and possesses the quality of being a standard is called the *dharmakāya*;
that which possesses the function of tranquil illumination is called *prajñā*;
and that which possesses the virtue of being free from entanglement is called *vimukti*.

This means that the very essence of liberation is that which can be taken as a model, and the essence that can be taken as a model is that which is capable of illumination; there is no separate essence that possesses these qualities.
According to the detailed explanations studied in the past, there are two types of interpretations:
The first [point] means that the essence of the perfectly consummate fruit is a true and wondrous existence; it is not like a mere provisional name, which possesses utility but lacks substantiality.
The second [point] means that Nirvana has no [independent] substance and is established by relying upon various virtues; how could it not be empty?
Huilang recounted Fayao’s words as follows:

"The meanings of birth-and-death and nirvana are divided into two. That is to say, because of the inversion of the twelve links of dependent origination, [birth-and-death] exists; yet, that very dependent origination is devoid of intrinsic nature, and this is called nirvana."
How could one wait until after being free from afflictions for there to be some "wondrous existence" that is not empty?
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Even if there were a dharma that surpassed nirvāṇa, it would still be said to be like an illusion and like a dream."
Furthermore, he cites the ancient interpretations of Xian, Ai, Zong, and others, which state:

"The myriad practices attain the fruit of ultimate perfection; the essence of this fruit is real. While its meanings are established according to its various attributes, it is not the case that a single entity is formed by the combination of these manifold meanings."
Faan said: "Although nirvana takes various virtues as its essence, it differs from the five aggregates forming a person. Why is this so?"
The person and the five aggregates are empty in terms of both their provisional and substantial natures;
yet while Nirvana is now empty, its manifold virtues are substantial. 3.
Narrating Original Existence. Third, according to Dao-sheng’s narrative: [The text continues with the narrative on original existence.]
Returning to the ultimate, one attains the source, yet it appears as if it has just begun.
What begins must necessarily end; this is why people are perpetually deluded.
If one traces its course, it is simply that I have just now realized it; it is not something perceived as existing in the present.
Sengliang’s preface states:
"Parinirvāṇa" is translated as "not" (bù) and is also called "non-existence" (wú).
"Par" means "birth" (shēng) and is also called "cause" (yīn).
Because it is not obtained through the cause of volitional action, it is "without cause.
Bao Liang’s preface states:
"In discerning birth and death, the eight sufferings are taken as the foundation."
To clarify nirvana, one takes permanence and bliss as its source.
Its wondrous essence is eternal and unmoving, while its function is constantly changing yet indestructible; it is without name or form, beyond the distinctions of the hundred negations.
Now, the purport of Nirvana is designated according to its functional application.

If one discusses the ultimate and the conventional, their two natures are fundamentally identical and their functions do not conflict; yet, when darkness departs and the conventional is exhausted, falsehood recedes and the ultimate is revealed, such that one becomes a Buddha with brilliant clarity.
The Preface to the *Fazhi* states:
"That which is profound and subtle is difficult to understand; it resides in what is 'originally existent' (*benyou*).
What is called 'originally existent' refers, in fact, to a mystical indication that future, separated ages exist; it does not mean that they exist in the present age."

As for the category of sentient beings with their innate consciousness, it already exists inherently even before the causal conditions for its source have been formed; therefore, it is said to be "originally existent.
Thus, since it does not depend on karmic conditions to initiate its beginning, it is not something newly created.
Therefore, it is said that this future [existence] is not the same as the other three periods of time, which must await the performance of karma before they can be considered existent.
Nevertheless, because the future has not yet arisen and has not yet been utilized, it requires a "revealing cause" (*jñāpaka-hetu*) before it can then respond.
Huilang recounted Fayao’s words as follows:
"The non-interruption of birth and death arises from the twelve links of dependent origination;
since these links lack intrinsic nature, they are themselves nirvana—how could they be something that begins to exist?"
4. Discourse on the Nameless (Discourse on the Nameless, Part Four). According to the consensus of the assembly:
Regarding that which has been traditionally detailed and studied, there are five kinds of interpretations.
The first is that the wondrous and ultimate Dharma-body is quiescent, unconditioned, and coextensive with True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The single characteristic is the absence of characteristics; how could it be reached by the power of words?
Although one may resort to speech to provide an exposition, though there is exposition, it transcends speech—just as one uses a finger to point toward the moon, yet the moon is not the finger.
Second, as for the principle that words are square while the truth is round, it is difficult to explain through discourse.
The Way of the Spirit is profound and obscure; it can be realized but cannot be described in words.
It is like the artisan Lun Pian’s carving of wheels: his subtle mastery could not be transmitted to his apprentice.
If even the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), being coarse and superficial, is difficult to describe, how much more so can the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)—profound and subtle—be named?
Third, that which is called "beyond words" refers to the stage of the Dharma-body, where the names of ordinary afflictions are utterly transcended.
Since its essence is the sublime existence of the Most Honored and Supreme One, how could it not be attained by means of the name "Most Honored and Supreme"?
Fourth, names are phenomena that bind one to appearances; if one invokes the ground where appearances bind, then the result will correspond to what was invoked.
If it is the ground of signlessness, although it may be attained through invocation, in the end it transcends all invocation.
Fifth, all dharmas are fundamentally beyond names and words.
Speaking from this perspective, how could it be merely the Dharma-body?
One may likewise designate birth-and-death as nirvana, and designate nirvana as birth-and-death.
Now that names have already been fixed, it is said that nirvana is distinguished from the name of birth-and-death precisely because it is worthy of esteem.
5. Explanation of the Title “The Great” (Dazhi), Part Five. According to Dao-sheng’s preface:
"If something does not exist in the present, then nothing could have preceded it to be called 'Great.
Since it is called 'Great,' it must therefore be eternal; that which is eternal must necessarily extinguish all burdens."
Sengliang said:
"The term 'Great' clarifies its constancy; it is also called the Great Self and Great Bliss, as will be explained in the subsequent text.
Sengzong said:
This refers to the greatness of the teaching and the greatness of the principle.
Regarding the greatness of the teaching: prior to this exposition, the discussion of cause, fruit, object, and practice had not yet reached full completion;
what is clarified today is the ultimate definitive meaning, and is therefore called "great."
Regarding "the Great Principle": in the past, the nirvana of the three vehicles was not the true ultimate; thus, within the context of the Principle, it was considered small.
Today, the liberation of body and wisdom exists beyond all burdens; thus, within the context of the Principle, it is considered great, and is therefore called "Great."
Baoliang said:
"Its essence and characteristics are boundless; therefore, it is called 'Great'. Fazhi said:
Since the principle corresponds to the name and the name does not deviate from the principle, both name and principle reach their ultimate perfection; therefore, it is called "Great. Fashuan said:
"Although there was Nirvana in the past, its essence and virtues were not yet complete, so it could not be termed 'Great'."
Today, his realization is perfected and his virtues are complete; therefore, he is called "Great. 6.
Explaining the Word "Sūtra" (Shì jīng zì). Section Six. According to the account by Sengliang:
"Sūtra" is the Hu-language pronunciation for *xiūduluó* (sūtra), a name that encompasses five meanings.
Sengzong stated:
"From the ordinary person to the sage, one passes through this principle.
Baoliang said:
This is the means by which scholars attain understanding; it is by means of this single character that the principles and patterns of an entire section are unified.
Zhi Xiu said: "In India, texts that expound upon principles are collectively termed *sūtra*."

It encompasses manifold meanings, such as "giving birth," "subtle manifestation," "gushing spring," "plumb line," and "flower garland"; as for the meaning of "sūtra" (jīng), it is but one among these.
Fazhi said: "There are two definitions.
The first is 'constant,' meaning words that accord with principle, which no sage can alter."
The second is called "means" (yō), referring to the means by which one departs from the state of an ordinary person and enters the state of a sage.
Fa'an said: Regarding the term "sūtra" (jīng), there are two ways of explaining its meaning:
The first is called "Constant" (Chang) and the second is called "Dharma.
In the foreign *sūtras*, there are many meanings; it is also called a "gushing spring" and also called a "plumb line."
Now, by using the meaning of "constancy" (*chang*) to replace that of "gushing spring," it clarifies that the flow pours forth without exhaustion.
By using the meaning of "Dharma" (*fa*) to replace that of "carpenter's line," it clarifies that when the compass and square are applied, the track and target do not vanish.
7. Examining the Intent of the Teachings, Part Seven. According to the account by Sengliang:
From the Bodhimaṇḍa until the twin śāla trees, the Tathāgata preached the Nirvāṇa three times; two of these were expedient means, and one was the ultimate truth.
What is this? First, the opening of the three culminations refers to the single means; it merely states that liberation is the body and wisdom of nirvāṇa, which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Within the two types of skillful means, although the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* speaks of the ultimate destruction of the three [vehicles], because body and wisdom remain, it is still conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The present teaching at the twin trees, however, holds that body and wisdom are themselves nirvāṇa; therefore, it is called the teaching of the ultimate state without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
Baoliang’s Preface states:

"As the faculties of sentient beings differ, the teachings are divided into five distinct categories. Just as beings may be deluded and their obstructions heavy such that they cannot yet find peace in the profound, expedient explanations were first opened to provide support for the present purpose of perfect and eternal truth."

In the past, I was instructed to train the mind so that it might gradually transcend the mundane to enter the Way; thus, I have thoroughly penetrated both wheels of the permanent and the impermanent, discerning that birth and death are the existence of non-existence, and nirvana is the non-existence of non-existence.

Having already established oneself in the truth and awakened to the principle, one recognizes suffering and emptiness and thereby severs delusion; yet, were it not for the cultivation of the Eightfold Path to give rise to the wisdom that accords with this principle, afflictions and delusions would not be dispelled, and birth and death would be difficult to eliminate.

Therefore, the rise of the present teaching reveals the wondrous essence of the divine spirit; thus, at the beginning of establishing its fundamental tenets, it employs the metaphor of the letter "I," which is neither vertical nor horizontal, differing from the former concepts of *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) and *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder).
Master Sengzong’s Preface states:
The reason why I have selected and recorded only "Liberation" (Jietuo) as the title of this scripture is twofold:
first, to clarify that the principle lies beyond all delusions; [and second, to show that it is the ultimate goal of practice].
Second, it refutes the former attachment to liberation.

In the past, those of the Lesser Vehicle were troubled by the arousal of body and cognition; they sought to extinguish this affliction by relying on liberation. Therefore, the present superior [teaching] is used to replace that of the past.
Zhi Xiu’s Preface states:

From the Tathāgata’s initial transformation at the Deer Park to the ultimate realization of his intent at Vulture Peak, he clarified only that the Way reaches its pinnacle when all traces are extinguished and that goodness necessarily leads to Bodhi; yet he did not distinguish that all sentient beings, possessing emotion and vital breath, are entirely equal to the Unsurpassed.
He merely spoke of the lifespan being long and far exceeding previous reckonings, but did not clarify that the Perfect Enlightenment is empty, tranquil, and profoundly indestructible.

This present sutra takes the ultimate, wondrous conditioned existence as its guiding manual and the eternally abiding Buddha-nature as its central tenet. It clarifies that for icchantikas, the true cause remains unaltered; it distinguishes the Dharma-body as the manifest, perfected fruit. This is what is called the supreme teaching without remainder and the ultimate, final discourse.
Section Eight: Analysis of the Chapters. Case Eight: Master Sengliang says:
Since the sūtra has not yet reached its conclusion, the current divisions may be categorized into four distinct sections:
first, the exhortation to inquire; second, the inquiry; third, the response to the inquiry; and fourth, the testimony of the Wheel of Dharma.
According to Tandai:
there are ten major divisions.
The first is the introductory exposition, which is the "Preface Chapter" (Xǔpǐn).
The second is the "Correct Exposition," spanning from the "Cunda Chapter" to the "Vajra-Body Chapter";
the third is the "Exposition on Circulation," spanning from the "Chapter on the Merits of Names" to the "Chapter on the Four Perversions";
and the fourth is the "Exposition on Buddha-nature," spanning from the "Tathāgata-nature Chapter" to the "Moon Simile Chapter."
The fifth section praises the efficacy of the sutra, spanning from the "Bodhisattva Chapter" to the "Manifesting Illness Chapter.
The sixth clarifies practice based on the sutra, which refers to the five practices (*pañca-caryā*).

The seventh explains the essence of practice, which carries the meaning of possessing merit; it takes the orientation toward the fruit of Buddhahood as the meaning of practice, and the sense of virtue arising from such effort constitutes the meaning of merit.
The eighth section is a critical analysis of the Buddha-nature explained above, which corresponds to the "Siṃhanāda-parivarta";

the ninth is likewise a critical analysis of Buddha-nature, extensively clarifying the principles elucidated from the "Vṛkṣarāja-parivarta" down to the present, citing the case of Sunakṣatra’s severing of his roots, which corresponds to the "Kāśyapa-parivarta";
and the tenth clarifies the propagation of the teaching, enjoining Kauṇḍinya to convert the ten non-Buddhists, spanning from the "Kauṇḍinya-parivarta" to the end of the sutra.
According to Tanxian, this sutra is broadly divided into two distinct parts: the former being concise and the latter being extensive.
Within the concise section, it is further divided into five segments:
The first is the "Introductory Chapter";
the second is the "Establishment of the Doctrine," which clarifies the causes and effects of eternal abiding, spanning from the "Chapter on Dhāraṇī" to the "Chapter on Lamentation";
the third is the "Questions," spanning from the "Chapter on Longevity" to the end of the questions.
The fourth response begins from the praise of Kāśyapa and continues through the end of the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly";
the fifth entrustment begins from "At that time, the great assembly addressed the Buddha" and concludes with the chapter.
Within the section on the Broad Exposition, it is divided into five parts:
first, the broad exposition of the fruit, which is the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness";
second, the broad exposition of the causes, which refers to the Five Practices.
The third is the extensive circulation, namely the "Chapter on the Ten Merits. The reason why the Radiant Light has come from afar is precisely to clarify this widespread propagation.
The fourth is the extensive exposition on the Buddha-nature, which comprises the two chapters "Lion's Roar" and "Kāśyapa";
the fifth is the extensive exposition on the entrustment, spanning from the "Kauṇḍinya" chapter to the end of the scripture.
According to Tanji:
"In general, there are three sections: first, the Section on Exhortation; second, the Section on Inquiry; and third, the Section on Response.
From 'Thus have I heard' up to Kāśyapa’s posing of the question constitutes the Section on Exhortation."
The section on the divisions of the response concludes with the answer given by Kauṇḍinya.
According to Sengzong,
there are five distinct sections throughout the beginning and end of this sutra.

second is the brief exposition of the doctrine of permanence, from the "Cunda Chapter" (*Cunda-parivarta*) through to the "Two Doctors Chapter" (*Dvaidhācintya-parivarta*);

third is the extensive clarification of eternal abiding, from the "Longevity Chapter" (*Āyuṣmat-parivarta*) through to the "Kāśyapa Chapter" (*Kāśyapa-parivarta*). The general outline of the objects, practices, causes, and effects has now been largely completed, and [the Buddha] is about to entrust [the teaching].
The fourth section first refutes the non-Buddhists, spanning from the "Kauṇḍinya Chapter" to the passage "Where is Ānanda?

Once the textual intent is concluded, there must be an entrustment; therefore, the fifth section concerns the person to whom the teaching is entrusted for its upholding, spanning from "Where is the bhikṣu Ānanda now? to the end of the sutra.

third, from the Buddha’s praise of Kāśyapa until the end of Kāśyapa’s response, the answers are given;
fourth, from the section beginning with Kauṇḍinya until the conclusion of the sutra, the entrustment for circulation is set forth.
The reason the first [chapter] serves as an exhortation to inquire is that this sutra takes question and answer as its primary tenet.

According to Daohui’s record,
this sutra is broadly divided into ten distinct sections.
The first is the introductory discourse, which is the "Introductory Chapter" (Xǔpǐn).
The second is the section on the Correct Teaching, from the "Cunda" chapter through the "Vajra-body" chapter;
the third is the section on the Propagation of the Teaching, from the "Merit of Names" chapter through the "Four Perversions" chapter;

and the fourth is the section on Buddha-nature, from the "Tathāgata-nature" chapter through the "Moon Simile" chapter, which clarifies that the reason one attains permanence is because of the primordially existing Buddha-nature.
The fifth is the praise of the sutra, which is the single chapter titled "Bodhisattva";

the sixth establishes the permanence [of the Buddha], clarifying that he manifests eating though he does not eat, manifests illness though he is not ill, and manifests extinction though he does not undergo extinction—this is the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness";
the seventh clarifies what is attained, namely that those who are free from illness do so by virtue of their practice—this refers to the five practices and ten merits.
The eighth section clarifies the meaning of the objective realm (*viṣaya*) for the sake of perfecting practice; it consists of the "Lion’s Roar" and the "Kāśyapa" chapters.
The ninth section refutes the doctrines of non-Buddhists; it is the "Kauṇḍinya" chapter.
The tenth section is the discourse on the entrustment (*parindanā*), beginning from the words "Where is Ānanda? and continuing to the end of the sutra.

The goodness first cultivated through practice is contrary to one's original evil nature; this is comparable to common laborers.
If they apply diligent effort, the harvest will be ten-thousandfold, just like farming with a well-trained ox.
According to Sengliang’s commentary:
The following passage serves as an analogy for the completion of the conditions for practicing *dāna*.
Internally, one possesses right view; externally, one’s body and speech are free from obstruction. Only when a Buddha accepts offerings can the *dharmakāya* be brought forth.
Sengzong said:
"It is like subduing the sevenfold evils of body and speech;
it is like a fertile field that is level and even."
According to Sengzong:
"Wisdom is likened to a field; one plows the field with an ox, and a field is considered excellent when it is level and even.
Now, by employing the goodness of body and speech to assist in the completion of mental karma, one thereby attains correct wisdom."
Baoliang said:

"A field possesses the power to produce, yet if it is not plowed by oxen, that power to produce will not be realized; this is analogous to how the karma of body and speech can bring to fruition the functions of the mental ground."
It is free from all saline wasteland, evil weeds, and desolate filth.
According to Sengliang:
this is like subduing the ninety-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*).
One only hopes for the rain from heaven.

when the Tathāgata accepts what is offered, the Dharma-body is thereby brought forth, just as moisture is produced by rain.

Regarding the phrase "taming the ox," it is a metaphor for [taming] the seven [faculties] of body and speech to rescue and reach infinite sentient beings suffering in affliction.
According to Sengliang:
"If my conduct is established, then sentient beings will receive deliverance."
Sengzong said:
"If what I have offered is surely accepted, then the same must be true for the offerings of the great assembly. Mingjun said:
If you accept my offerings, you should likewise remain in this world for my sake;
for if there is a Buddha in the world, sentient beings will receive salvation.
Although the offerings I now present are meager, I hope they may suffice to satisfy the Tathāgata and his great assembly.
Huilang submitted this petition:
"Since what I have spoken is so meager, I hope that by relying upon your majestic spiritual power, it may universally satisfy the great assembly.
Now, being without a master, without kin, and without refuge, I pray that you will look upon me with compassion, as you did for Rāhula."
According to Tanji:
