even though the lamp is extinguished and the snake is no longer seen, one ultimately does not enter the room.
The emptiness of the nature of all phenomena is seen through concentration; although one may fall back from concentration and no longer see it, one does not give rise to afflictions.
Some, hearing that one falls back from concentration, claim that even the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) falls back;
others, hearing that the outflow-free state does not fall back, claim that concentration likewise does not fall back.
Sengzong said: "This is the fourth type of contentious debate.
From the four foundations of mindfulness downward, one has not yet attained right faith, and thus there may occasionally be regression."
Once one has entered the stage of *uṣmagata*, one never regresses, continuing until the attainment of arhatship.
If this is untainted (*anāsrava*), there is no regression; if it is tainted (*sāsrava*), there may be regression.
Those of dull faculties regress, while those of sharp faculties do not.

The nature of the untainted (anāsrava) arises from the illumination of principle; once attained, it is never lost. One merely regresses from tainted concentration, such that the untainted does not manifest before one.
Baoliang said:
"Arhats possess both sharp and dull faculties.

From the sixth stage of abiding onward, they have completely suppressed and severed the afflictions that obstruct meditative concentration; the afflictions pertaining to rebirth no longer arise, just as scorched charcoal can never become wood again. However, there remains only the ignorance that obstructs meditative concentration."
Since these have already been subdued and severed, if one of sharp faculties emerges from untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-dhyāna*) and wishes to re-enter it, they can do so immediately.

However, for one of dull faculties, it is difficult to re-enter after emerging from contemplation; because they must apply further deliberate attention (*manasikāra*) to enter, this is termed "retrogression" (*hāni*).
Alternatively, an Arhat may regress and give rise to the mental deliberations (*vitarka*) of the desire realm, thereby becoming a Srotāpanna.
As for those said not to regress, it means their meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) also does not regress; this is why a dispute arises.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu named Gautamīputra who proclaimed: "The Tathāgata has definitively taught that there is no falling back.
According to Sengliang:
Gautamīputra was an anāgāmin who fell back from the fixed state six times, yet he did not exhaust his outflows.
The seventh [type of practitioner] commits suicide because he fears losing his attained realization; yet, before he dies, his outflows (āsrava) are completely exhausted.
The Māra King, thinking that this practitioner of the path has passed away, circles his corpse in search of his consciousness (vijñāna).
Being unable to obtain it, he said to the Buddha:
"Your disciple died before his outflows were exhausted.
The Buddha replied:
"This person has forever uprooted the faculty of sensation and has already entered nirvana.
This was cited as proof for the division of the six types of arhats.
Sengzong said:

Regarding the principle of the possibility of falling away from the untainted (anāsrava), this is cited as the authority: namely, that there is falling away from both the tainted and the untainted aspects of the fruit of Arhatship.
"Good son! In the sutras, I have stated that the body of the Tathāgata reaches the state where it is definitively taught that the Buddha-body is an unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma)."
According to Sengliang:
"Śrāvakas and Buddhas are alike in their nirvāṇa; they differ only in that [the former] involves moment-to-moment arising and ceasing, while [the latter] is non-arising and non-ceasing.
Those who are not yet learners take the name 'Vajra' as their learning; when the knowledge of all modes first arises, it is called 'beyond-learning' (aśaikṣa)."
The Dharma-body is neither born nor extinguished; it possesses no dual characteristics.
As for the Buddha’s appearing in the world or not appearing, he remains eternally constant and immovable: he appears through response, and does not appear when there is no response.
However, it should then be eternally neither arising nor ceasing.

Those who do not understand my intention claim that things must be definitively either conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), such that what is unconditioned is eternal and what is conditioned is impermanent.
Sengzong said: "This is the fifth point of contention.
When one hears it taught that [the Buddha] has entered extinction, one assumes he lacks a Dharma-body."
Hearing that the Dharma-body is imperishable, one concludes that its manifested traces are likewise eternal.
My previous discussion regarding the absence of self and the separation of the body was based on the meaning of the present state.
Baoliang said: "If one hears that the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is impermanent, one will assume there is no dharma-body (dharmakāya);
yet if one hears it is eternally abiding, one will again fall into the same views as the non-Buddhists."
The two explanations diverge from one another, and thus a dispute arises.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra-śikṣā-bhāṣya*, Fascicle 64;
*Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra-śikṣā-bhāṣya*, Fascicle 65.
The sixth explanation concerns the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), whether they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The seventh explanation concerns whether the mind is said to be eternal (*nitya*) or impermanent (*anitya*).
The eighth explanation concerns whether the pleasures of the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*) obstruct the Path or do not obstruct it.
The ninth [section] explains that the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma may exist either in the Desire Realm or within the Three Realms.
The tenth [section] explains that some claim giving consists solely of mental action, while others claim it consists of all five aggregates.
The eleventh [section] explains that there may be three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), or there may be no three unconditioned phenomena.
The twelfth explanation states that there may be derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) or there may be no derived matter;
the thirteenth explanation states that there is non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) or there is no non-informative matter;
the fourteenth explanation states that there may be mental factors (*caitta*) or there may be no mental factors.
Fifteenth: Explaining the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*), or alternatively, the five, six, seven, or eight states of existence.
Sixteenth: Explaining the meaning of a partial *upāsaka*.
Seventeenth: Explaining the meaning of losing the precepts through committing a grave offense, or not losing them.
The eighteenth explanation states that those who have attained the four fruits of the path become Buddhas, while others state that they do not.
The nineteenth explanation states that Buddha-nature exists within sentient beings, yet it also exists apart from sentient beings.
The twentieth explanation concerns whether there are Buddhas of the ten directions or no Buddhas of the ten directions. From the third section of the Kāśyapa Chapter: "Good son!..."
In my sutras, it is asked: "What is meant by saying that reaching the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda) is necessarily conditioned (saṃskṛta)?
According to Sengliang:
"The conditioned is impermanent; the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is permanent."
There are two kinds:
first, the impermanence of cessation and extinction, which does not belong to the category of sentient beings;
second, the impermanence of non-cessation, which refers to the twelve links of dependent origination.
Permanence is also of two kinds:
permanence characterized by arising and ceasing refers to the twelve links of dependent origination;
permanence characterized by non-arising and non-ceasing refers to nirvana.
Thus, these twelve links of dependent origination are both permanent and impermanent.
Yet, some, upon hearing that dependent origination involves arising and ceasing, claim it perishes along with grass and trees;
others, hearing it does not arise or cease, claim it is of one and the same character as nirvana, thereby giving rise to contentious debates.
Sengzong said: "This is the sixth point of contention.
If one discusses the correct principle, the mutual generation of the twelve links of dependent origination reaches its ultimate fulfillment only with the Buddha."

Now, the reason why holding [the view] that conditioned phenomena exist leads to error is that, from birth to old age and death, they would be severed and no longer continue, which contradicts the principle of continuity;
whereas "unconditioned" means there is no severance whatsoever.
Baoliang said: "The twelve links of dependent origination are indeed conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

As for why they are called 'conditioned' and thus give rise to dispute, it is because they do not constitute a conditioned continuity of cause and effect; rather, each link is held to be severed and extinguished within its own substance, such that no further causal relationship remains."
On another occasion, I told the bhikṣus that whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, the nature and characteristics [of reality] abide eternally.
According to Sengliang:
"Because the succession is without difference, it is called 'eternal'."

"Good son! There are twelve links of dependent origination that do not arise from conditions, up to the statement that the twelve links of dependent origination are definitively unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
According to Sengliang:..."
Although four propositions are cited, only the first is taken to explain the cause for the arising of delusions.
"Not arising from conditions" means that it has not yet conjoined with conditions.
"Arising from conditions but not being the twelvefold dependent origination" is stated as "not" because it does not possess all twelve links.
Baoliang said:

"The second phrase states that there are twelve links of dependent origination that do not arise from conditions; this refers to the twelve branches of the future world, which are said not to arise from conditions simply because they have not yet arisen.
Yet some claim they do not arise from conditions because they are eternal."

This text is based on the teachings of the past; however, those who adhere to them each speak with partiality, asserting that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) have no further continuity. Since both schools thus deviate from the truth, they dispute one another.
"Good son! In my sutras, it is said that all sentient beings reach the point of proclaiming: 'The Tathāgata says the mind is certainly permanent.
According to Sengliang:"
Because form possesses the characteristic of change, it is said to perish; yet because the mind lacks such a characteristic of change, it is said to be permanent.
Upon hearing that form perishes while the mind is permanent, some then claim that the mind is neither born nor extinguished, extending this assertion from the lower realms up to the highest heavens.
Sengzong said: "This is the seventh point of contention.

If we discuss the correct principle, according to ultimate reality (dharmatā), a phenomenon perishes first and then arises; however, according to conventional designation (prajñapti), it remains one and the same from beginning to end."

Alternatively, upon hearing it said that the mind ascends, they fail to understand its continuity and claim that this mind is permanent and does not perish, asserting that it migrates upward to receive rebirth.
Son of good family, at one time, for the sake of Bimbisāra and others, I proclaimed: "The Tathāgata says that the mind is definitively severed."
According to Sengliang, he said:
"Upon hearing that the five aggregates all perish, one immediately assumes that the mind is also like form, subject to distinctions such as large and small, long and short.
Sengzong said:
Upon hearing the teaching on impermanence, they claim that when this aggregate-body is discarded, the mind is also severed and extinguished, never to continue again.

Baoliang said: "To speak of permanence is to say it is absolutely non-extinguishing; to speak of annihilation is to say there is suddenly no continuity. It is for this reason that the dispute arises."
"Good son! In my sūtras, I have said that when my disciples reach the point of discussing the enjoyment of the five desires, it certainly obstructs the Right Path.
According to Sengliang:
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) take the severance of worldly affairs as the Way; therefore, they lie in ashes and eat husks.
The Buddha-dharma is not like this.
Yet some, hearing that desire does not obstruct [the Path], claim that even when a mind of desire manifests before them, it likewise does not obstruct the Path.
Hearing that the mind of desire is an obstacle, they then claim that things such as incense and flowers can also obstruct the Path;
thus, they give rise to contention. Good son!
In my sutras, it is taught that from the distancing of afflictions up to the attainment of the Supreme Dharma (agradharma) occurs within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
According to Sengliang,
this refers to the fruit of Arhatship.
The Arhat has no abode in the desire realm.

In the three realms, one is able to cultivate the foremost dharma and enter the path of seeing the truths, with the sole exception of the single stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

The [first] three of the lower [realms] are all capable [of this], yet the Buddha spoke of them differently according to the specific circumstances; thus, some individuals, adhering to what they heard in their own particular way, developed disputes through partiality.
When one cultivates the first dharma, it is called "separation" because it can suppress the fetters of views;
however, because the Four Truths have not yet been seen and the fetters have not yet been completely severed, one has not yet attained liberation and remains in the First Dhyāna.

Regarding the attainment of the fourth dhyāna: in the concentration of the desire realm, wisdom is abundant while concentration is meager; in the formless concentrations, concentration is abundant while wisdom is meager; whereas in the form-realm concentrations, concentration and wisdom are balanced and thus easy to employ. Therefore, it is described as the most accessible state.
Alternatively, one might claim that neither the higher nor the lower [stages] are capable [of such attainment].
Regarding those who have attained the fruit of Anāgāmin, this sutra contains no teaching regarding "leap-over" (vyutkrāntaka) attainment.

As for those who have attained the third fruit (Anāgāmin), having already suppressed and severed the fetters of the three lower realms through the three emptinesses, their untainted contemplation (anāsrava-darśana) is so sharp upon seeing the True Truths that they do not remain in the first fruit even if they pass through it.
Now I have merely described his place of residence. Sengzong said:
"This is the ninth point of contention."

If one discusses the correct principle, the mind of the desire realm and the minds of the four dhyānas are all capable of performing the contemplation of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

It is also possible for the three formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) to possess it; however, the mental states of these stages are difficult to employ, and for this reason, people do not follow what is difficult but mostly take what is easy.
In each stage, one has entirely subdued the fetters; however, at that time, true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*) has not yet been attained.
If one possesses sharp faculties, even while remaining in the desire realm, one is able to project the mind fully into the higher stages and can subdue the fetters of those higher stages.
Those of dull faculties may not necessarily be able to do so; it must arise in successive stages.
Because [the Buddha] was speaking for those of sharp faculties, he stated that the Supreme Mundane Dharma (agradharma) exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Failing to understand the Buddha’s intention, they claim it belongs exclusively to the desire realm and cannot employ a mind belonging to the dhyāna stages.

If one hears it said that the contemplation of the four dharmas is practiced within the four dhyānas, this is because [the practitioner] relies on the mind of the fundamental stage; that is to say, they exclusively do not employ the desire realm, as doing so would deviate from the Middle Way. This is why there is dispute.
Baoliang said:
"Speaking in terms of principle, when the mind of the three realms is exhausted, one attains the foremost dharma (*agra-dharma*).

Even if one has not yet attained the eight dhyānas, but has merely attained the 'lightning-flash concentration' (*vidyut-prabhā-samādhi*) of the desire realm, one may still employ this concentration to practice the contemplation of the emptiness of nominal dharmas (*prajñapti-dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*)."
Therefore, the Buddha taught that such a person acts with a mind belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
There are those who, having attained the eight dhyānas, take the "emptiness of dharmas" (*dharmasunyatā*) as a mere provisional designation (*prajñapti*).

Furthermore, there are others who, having previously suppressed their fetters up to the three empties (*trisuññatā*), encounter a noble one (*ārya*) in that stage and employ the concentration of the three empties to perform the "first dharma" (*ānulomikī kṣānti*).
Yet some do not understand; hearing that it is produced by a mind of the desire realm, they claim it cannot be produced in the two higher realms;
hearing that it can be produced in the three higher realms, they further claim it cannot be produced in the desire realm—thus, a dispute arises.
Zhixiu said: "Both realms can attain the foremost dharma.
Mingjun noted:
All that has been explained above follows the principles of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.

If one follows the principles of the *Abhidharma-saṃyukta*, only two elements can be produced, for those four meditative absorptions of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhyāna*) cannot produce them at all.
Why is this? It means that from the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) upward, one still cannot take it as an object;
how much less could the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), which merely resemble the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), ever become so?
The meaning of "eating characteristics" is something understood only by those of detailed wisdom and sagacity. Good son!
In my sutras, among the four kinds of giving, it is declared that the Tathāgata says: "Giving consists solely of the mind."
According to Sengliang:
The actions of body, speech, and mind are all the substance of giving. If they are pure or impure, then the merit will be substantial or meager.
Purity necessarily arises from faith; thus, there must be purity of intention.
On the first three days:
one person possesses both purities;
the other two possess mutual faith in one another.
Although there are distinctions of superior and inferior, all may be called "pure.

Yet some, upon hearing that pure giving arises from faith—and since faith is a mental action (manas-karma)—conclude that the implements of giving must reside within the mind; it is for this reason that they give rise to dispute.
“Good son! At one time I also spoke thus, up to declaring: ‘The Buddha taught that giving is itself the five aggregates.
According to Sengliang’s commentary:”
The Buddha spoke of the fruit within the context of the cause, referring to the five kinds of giving.
Some may hear this and think that food alone constitutes the act of giving; however, all external objects that can be given are indeed acts of giving.
Since the phenomena subsumed within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) have been completely severed and exhausted, it is said that giving is itself the five aggregates.
Sengzong remarked:
"This is the tenth polemical treatise."

From the perspective of righteousness, the mind is the master of giving and other virtues, while form assists in their accomplishment; body and speech assist the mind, yet body and speech are not themselves the dharma of sentient consciousness.
Upon hearing it said that two types of action are pure, they claim that only mental karma is involved and that body and speech are irrelevant;
upon hearing it said that giving consists of five matters, they claim that it is merely physical form and not mind—thus they engage in further dispute.
Baoliang said:

"If there is one who has long practiced the Way and perfected the mind of renunciation, practicing it at all times, for such a person the Buddha taught that giving is itself the intention (*manas*), and it does not depend upon body or speech to be accomplished."
Furthermore, there are those whose roots of goodness are weak and inferior, who must rely on the assistance of body and speech before they can perform an act of giving.

If one does not move the body or speak, but merely gives rise to a mental thought, the karmic action of giving is not accomplished; for such people, the Buddha taught that the "requisites of giving" are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Alternatively, one might misinterpret the Buddha’s intention: if one hears it said that giving consists solely of the mind, one might conclude that it has no relation to body or speech;
yet when it is stated that [giving] possesses the five aggregates, it necessarily requires the completion of the three types of action (trikarma).
As each of these two positions is partial, they give rise to contentious debate. Good son!
At one time, I proclaimed the teaching of *nirvāṇa*, up to declaring that the Buddha taught there are no three [vehicles] and no unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
According to Sengliang, the Buddha taught the two truths. Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are causes, and these causes are of two kinds:
first, those with functional efficacy; second, those without functional efficacy.
That which has no functional utility refers to the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
That which possesses functional utility refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Some, hearing that *nirvāṇa* can sever birth and death, claim that there exists an unconditioned phenomenon which is subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Hearing that there is no such dharma, they claim that there is no nirvana capable of severing birth and death, thereby giving rise to contentious debate.
When a lamp is extinguished, it is simply the cessation of light; there is no further "dharma of extinction" that arises.
Nirvana is also like this: it is simply the cessation of afflictions, with no further phenomena arising.
Because the afflictions have ceased, birth and death do not continue; this is the function of non-existence, which is called space.
This is the emptiness of general characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā); therefore, it is called "constant" and "pervasive.

The emptiness of horses and so forth in the world is the emptiness of specific characteristics (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā); this too takes the non-existence of phenomena as its emptiness, being employed as a metaphor.
Because they possess distinct characteristics, they are neither eternal nor universal.
Regarding "cessation not through the condition of wisdom" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): cessation through the condition of wisdom is supramundane and untainted (*anāsrava*);
cessation not through the condition of wisdom is mundane and untainted.

Although there is a distinction between the mundane and the supramundane, the meaning of cessation is permanent and identical to space; thus, it is designated as one of the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Non-Buddhists do not attain the untainted severance of fetters; even when their fetters are extinguished, they arise again, and therefore this cannot be called permanent.
Sengzong said: "This is the eleventh point of contention.
From the perspective of the correct principle, it is not that the three unconditioned phenomena do not exist; rather, they are simply distinguished as three separate dharmas."
Baoliang said:
Some maintain that within emptiness there is no substance and nothing can be differentiated; it is merely a single emptiness, devoid of the three unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Within this, the Buddha’s intention may be described as both existent and non-existent: it is called "non-existent" because emptiness has no distinct dharma apart from itself, and it is called "existent" because one seeks it by following its meaning.
"Good son! At one time, for the sake of Maudgalyāyana, I went as far as to proclaim that the Tathāgata said there is nirvāṇa.
According to Sengliang:
What is called "nirvāṇa" refers to the words and phrases [of the teaching].
What the sages have trodden upon is called their "track.
That which is never again lost or regressed is called "ultimate."
The absence of the eight sufferings is what is meant by "fearlessness.
The one who cures the disease of birth and death is the Great Master.
The fruit-wisdom, patience, non-obstruction, and samādhi are all names according to their various distinct meanings.
That which shares the same characteristics as the Dharma is called the Great Dharma Realm (Mahādharmadhātu).
The severing of old age, sickness, and death is called the flavor of ambrosia (amṛtarasa).
That which cannot be grasped is called difficult to see.
Furthermore, at another time, for the sake of Maudgalyāyana, I went so far as to definitively state that space and the unconditioned exist.
According to Sengliang:
"If there were an intrinsic nature, that nature would be indestructible."
Because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is called "not firm.
That which is named "empty space" is without nature and without phenomena; yet, as phenomena have utility and it shares the same nature as empty space, it is given that name.

Regarding "the food turning back as it descends," this explains that the two—existence (bhava) and non-existence (abhāva)—mutually seek one another; when the food cannot descend and the sound does not issue forth, because there is neither existence for the food to descend nor non-existence for the sound to issue, this explains the function of emptiness (śūnyatā).
Alternatively, one may hear that emptiness has utility, meaning there are dharmas that are empty, which are subsumed under the dharma-base (dharmāyatana) and the form-base (rūpāyatana).
Furthermore, at another time, for the sake of Maudgalyāyana, [the Buddha] spoke up to the definitive teaching on existence as cessation not conditioned by wisdom (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
According to Sengliang:
"That which is extinguished by means of wisdom-conditions" refers to that which does not arise from supramundane, outflow-free (anāsrava) wisdom.

From the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata) and Summits (mūrdhan) up to the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma), these are mundane yet outflow-free, and they permanently sever the retribution of the three evil realms.
Baoliang said: "If it is extinguished by the conditions of wisdom, it is also called the unconditioned of the conditions of wisdom.
Since emptiness contains no substance, it may further differ from physical space; thus, it is also termed the unconditioned of space."
Since there is nothing further to be counted within space, it is termed "unconditioned through non-enumeration.

Those who do not understand this meaning, upon hearing "non-existence," fail to follow the sense that there are three [types]; yet upon hearing "existence," they claim that each of the three has a distinct essence.
Because one grasps at things by way of their appearances, disputes arise. Good son!
At another time, for the sake of Bāpaka, I spoke with definitive certainty, saying that form consists of the four great elements.
According to Sengliang’s commentary:

Regarding that which is called "form" (rūpa) among the four great elements (mahābhūta), there are five categories of form-dharmas. The four great elements are provisional; by speaking of the four, all instances of seeing are exhausted.
Sound is produced from the four great elements; by citing the root, the derivative is encompassed.

To definitively state that form (*rūpa*) consists of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) implies that wherever there is a locus of form, the four great elements must always coexist. This would mean that fire exists within water, coldness within boiling water, and even sound in the air possesses the four great elements; such a view misses the essential point.
Sengzong said: "This refers to the twelve points of contention.

If one considers this to be the correct principle, then color, odor, taste, and tangibility constitute the four great elements (mahābhūta), and these four great elements in turn constitute the five sense organs, such as the eye."
Although there are said to be fourteen kinds of matter, if categorized by their essential nature (*dhātu*), they do not exceed the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
If the four great elements are the cause and the five sense organs are the effect, since the cause cannot exist apart from the effect, one may say that [the organs] are produced by the cause.

Upon hearing it said that the four great elements constitute "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa), they do not understand how these are subsumed within their own nature; they claim that there are only the four great elements and no other form.

Upon hearing it said that what is produced is created by the four great elements, they argue that the sense organs can be said to be created from the great elements, for there can be no effect apart from its cause.
Even down to the term "sudden-slip" (*huòhuá*), if one follows what is clarified in the *Catuḥmahābhūta-varga*, none of these [terms] differentiate the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*).

Failing to discern this statement—that past four great elements produce the form (*rūpa*) of the three periods of time—it is said that the present bodily and vocal karma exists because it is derived from them; that they are able to produce it because of the powerful strength of the thirty-four great forces of the past; and that the present produces two periods while the future produces only one period.
Failing to grasp the Buddha’s intent, they further engage in contentious debate.
Baoliang said:
Some claim that the four great elements possess powerful strength capable of creating form and so forth, whereas form and so forth possess inferior strength and cannot create the four great elements.
He constantly devised this scheme.
On another occasion, the Buddha was preaching to the bhikṣus that the five aggregates (skandhas) are entirely empty, asking: "What is form (rūpa)?"
Form is itself the four great elements;
thus it is said that the four great elements cannot produce form.
Furthermore, when it is said at another time that the four great elements produce form—referring to such things as squareness and roundness—this is merely a cause based on internal mutual dependence.
Those who hear this teaching will say that the four great elements definitely can create matter.
However, if one discusses the Middle Way or the correct principle, one should say that they both create and do not create.
Why is this? Because various conventional forms, such as square and round, arise based on the four great elements, they are also said to be "created.
Regarding the six preceding great elements and the subsequent four great elements, there is no further creation.
The five sense objects are likewise; because the coarse is formed from the subtle, they may also be called "form derived from form.
Since that which precedes is form and that which follows is also form, it is said that one does not produce the other.
People do not understand this; upon hearing that one has made [an image], they all feel compelled to make one, and upon hearing that one has not made one, they all believe no one should make one.
By making both extremes, they lose the Middle Way, which is why disputes arise.
"Good son! I have further said that, for example, because of a mirror, there arises what is called 'derived matter' (bhautika-rūpa), which is like an echo or a reflection.
According to Sengliang:

The four great elements are provisional designations that possess utility: earth provides stability, wind provides motion, water provides moisture, and fire provides maturation; thus, form is able to grow and develop, appearing like a reflection in a mirror.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they conclude that because the four great elements exist, there must be derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
According to Sengliang, however,
the statement that the four great elements "can create" means they are not themselves the created.
Form (rūpa) is that which is produced, not that which produces.
There may be the four great elements (mahābhūta) without the form they produce.
According to Sengliang:
It is said that the four great elements (mahābhūta) are provisional, being produced by real dharmas.

The real dharmas, such as form (rūpa), are not themselves produced; yet the Buddha spoke of "producing the producer," for the four great elements also produce derived matter (upādāyarūpa). This is like a bundle of bamboo that stands upright by supporting one another.
The two aforementioned schools are both biased attachments; neither has grasped the Buddha’s intent. Good son!
Once in the past, Prince Bodhi went to [a place where] he was not called "one who has lost the precepts," yet he was still called "one who maintains the precepts."
According to Sengliang:
"Non-action (avijñapti) is the essence of the precepts.
This refers to the ten wholesome precepts; among the seven branches of body and speech, non-action arises from the manifested form (vijñapti-rūpa), and this non-action constitutes form.
The remaining three do not arise from volitional action (*abhisamskāra*) and are therefore not called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). Sengzong said:
"This is the thirteenth disputation."
If one discusses the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no such thing as non-action that is not of the mind.
Although it is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*), it cannot be said not to exist.
This is the nature of wholesome dharmas that opposes evil; because the cause is spoken of in terms of the result, it is said that non-action is form.
It is obtained by arising from form; it is merely named after its cause.
Because some hear this and do not understand it, they claim that non-action (avijñapti) is itself form.
Baoliang said:

Regarding the statement that for Prince Bodhi, "this non-action is form": if it were simply stated that the mind itself is the precept, the prince would have thought that whenever an evil thought arose, all the precepts he had received would be lost, leaving him with no precepts to maintain. Therefore, it is said that one obtains the non-action precepts through the seven branches of body and speech.
Those who misinterpret the Buddha’s intention claim that the precepts are simply non-action (*akṛti*) and require no further mental engagement.
They further assert that the precepts are merely the restraint of unwholesome dharmas; thus, if the mind does not commit evil, that itself constitutes the precepts.
Upon hearing this explanation, he claimed that there is no such thing as non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) at all.
This is why a dispute arose.

By what cause and condition is it called non-informative matter? It is not a different kind of matter; it is not a cause that produces a different kind of matter, nor is it an effect produced by a different kind of matter.
According to Sengliang:

"That which is not a cause distinct from matter" means that the performance of actions by body and speech is of the nature of matter (*rūpa-dharma*), consisting of the three types—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

Precepts take wholesome action as their cause; since wholesome action differs from the unwholesome and the indeterminate, it is called "distinct from matter" and "having a cause distinct from matter."
Regarding "not producing a result that is a different color from its cause": there is no production of a result that is a different color from its cause.
To say that "non-difference" is the cause means there is no such result as a result identical [to it].
Sengzong said:
"That which is not a cause distinct from form means that form itself is the substance of non-action (*avijñapti*).
If other forms do not give rise to non-action, they are not causes of non-action; this is the case with neutral bodily and vocal actions, as well as the forms of mountains and rivers."
Since it has already been stated that they are not the causes for the distinct material forms (*rūpa*), the distinct material forms are likewise not their effects.

If the wholesome material forms of body and speech were able to produce non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), then those distinct material forms would be its cause, and the distinct material forms would also be its effect.
Because it is attained by following wholesome form (*rūpa*), it is called "unconditioned" (*avijñapti*).
Due to a lack of understanding, some then claim that unconditioned action is itself form.
Baoliang said:
"Neither is it a cause distinct from form": "distinct from form" refers to the mind; this clarifies that the mind alone does not serve as the cause.

"Nor is it a fruit distinct from its cause": this precept is also not solely the fruit of the mind; it must be the combined functioning of both form and mind to be designated as the goodness of the precept.
Daohui’s Record states:

This clarifies that if one wishes to give rise to non-informative action (*avijñapti*), one must first properly align the body, join the palms, and manifest an extraordinary appearance; only then can one bring forth this fruit of non-informative action.
Zhi Xiu said: "The mind is not the body or speech; this is what is meant by 'not being of a different nature' (fei yise).
Since the body and speech have no active agency and do not arise from it [the mind], it is said that they do not take 'being of a different nature' as their cause."

"Not producing the effect of a different kind of form" means that it does not act as a cause for the mind to produce an effect; thus, it is said that it does not produce the effect belonging to the category of causes that are of a different kind of form.
Huirang provides a separate interpretation, stating:
"Non-action is itself a different kind of form; this means that if something is not the cause of a different kind of form, then it will not produce the effect of a different kind of form."
"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they will cry out, 'The Buddha has said that there is such a thing as unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa).
According to Sengliang:..."
The Buddha’s intention is non-action and is not form; yet because it arises dependent upon form, it is designated as "form" according to its cause.
Failing to understand the Buddha’s intention, one might claim that non-action is the nature of form. Good son!
In other sutras, I have spoken thus, up to the point of definitively declaring that there is no such thing as "unmanifest form" (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
According to Sengliang:
"The vow not to commit evil gives rise to the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*), which is able to obstruct unwholesome dharmas."

One who does not commit evil is called a keeper of the precepts. When one does not commit evil, the non-action alone arises; because the nature of the precepts is luminous and pure, it is called "keeping the precepts.

If one gives rise to the commission of evil, the precepts coexist with evil, and the precepts are no longer luminous and pure; because this violates one's original vow, it is not called "keeping the precepts."

Failing to understand the Buddha’s intention, they hear it said that "non-action" (avijñapti) does not arise, and they conclude that there is no further arising of formal action (vijñapti), nor is there any non-action. Good son!
In my sūtras I have made such statements as these, up to the point where it is said that all ordinary worldlings are likewise so.
According to Sengliang’s commentary:
The sutras state that suffering and pleasure are governed by the mind.
The mind possesses both delusion and understanding; delusion is termed ignorance (*avidyā*), while understanding is termed right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).
Right view is the cause of happiness, while ignorance is the root of suffering; these two are distinct capacities of the mind.
They are established as numerical factors [of the path], and the five aggregates are suffering arising from ignorance, which explains the fault of delusion.
Sengzong said:
"The fourteenth is the dispute concerning whether mental factors (caitta/caitasika) exist or do not exist."
If we discuss the correct principle, the mind and its numerical aspects both exist and do not exist.
To say they have number means they arise in a sequence of before and after.
To say they have no number means they do not exist simultaneously at one and the same time.
Baoliang said:

"The Buddha taught this all at once; it makes no distinction between ordinary people and sages. All five aggregates arise because of ignorance, and the same applies even to the twelve links of dependent origination."

There are those who do not understand and say that this is merely ignorance; they claim that within it there is no further arising of cause and effect, but rather that it is simply a single entity that remains eternally as it is.
They merely employ different names and different explanations, asserting that while there are these twelve links, there are no mental factors (caitta). Zhi Xiu said:
"It is because the Buddha spoke of the twelve links of dependent origination and the two stages of cause and effect that these two schools have given rise to such attachments."
First, the causes of the past are clarified; therein, three things deviate from the norm:
first, from the link of ignorance (*avidyā*), the links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) extend further;
second, the link of formations (*saṃskāra*) is transformed and designated as "existence" (*bhava*).
Third, regarding the fruit, the name of the cause is applied to it.
Next, the five fruits are distinguished; there are five differences among them:
first, the transformation of consciousness into feeling.
Second, it is the case of designating the cause by the name of the result;
third, it is the detailed exposition of the various members following name-and-form;
fourth, it is the abbreviated treatment of the two members of contact and sensation.
Fifth, regarding the exposition based on the link of sensation (*vedanā*), this refers to the name of the fruit.
Alternatively, for those who maintain that mental factors (*caitasika*) do not exist, he next explains three causes and two fruits.
In explaining these three causes, two points deviate from the norm:
First, the branch of sensation (vedanā) is preceded by the emergence of visual consciousness and the other [sensory consciousnesses];
second, the name "transformative activity" (pariṇāma-karma) is applied.
Regarding these two results, two matters are modified from their ordinary state:
First, the *jāti* (birth) link is changed to *vijñāna* (consciousness);

second, the *jarāmaraṇa* (old age and death) link is expanded to include the names of various other links, because it is argued that *saṃjñā* (perception) and so forth are not identical to *sparśa* (contact).
Some, on this basis, maintain that mental factors (*caitasika*) arise simultaneously with the primary mind.
Daohui’s Record states:
"The differentiation between preceding and succeeding moments of mind is what is called 'mental factors' (caitta).
If one reckons that these preceding and succeeding moments are still but a single mind, then there would be no mental factors at all; this too is an error."
If one says that within a single moment there are distinct mental factors (*caitasika*) arising together, this too is an error.
One should know that from ignorance (*avidyā*) arises craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and that this craving extends through to existence (*bhava*); thus, these are ignorance, craving, and grasping (*upādāna*).
According to Sengliang’s commentary:

This teaching concerns the afflictions (*kleśa*) manifest in the present life; it clarifies that their numerical categories do not constitute separate entities, but arise directly from conditions, being classified as four based on their varying degrees of gravity.
Why is this? When the mind does not clearly comprehend its objects and fails to discern what is wholesome from what is unwholesome, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Clinging to what is wholesome and thereby giving rise to defilement is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The nature of craving and seeking is called *upādāna* (clinging).
The arising of bodily and verbal karma is called *bhava* (existence).

As for why it is said that these are "identical," their original names are not diminished; rather, they are designated differently based on their emphasis. Their essential natures are established concurrently, yet they are enumerated separately for the sake of distinction.
Sengzong said:
"If one discusses the sequence of cause and effect arising in succession, then the preceding cause and the subsequent effect do not exist simultaneously.

However, there are cases where they do not necessarily follow a sequential order; for instance, ignorance acts as the cause for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and there are instances where coarse afflictions give rise again to subtle ones, even up to the point where craving and sensation exhaust themselves yet still possess the principle of further production and origination."
This is the sequential arising of conditions.

As for "ignorance is craving" and "craving is [ignorance]," from beginning to end it is one and the same spiritual consciousness (*śuddha-vijñāna*). Although they differ as cause and effect, they cannot be separated; therefore, it is said that they are identical.
From "there is birth" up to "one should know that this is feeling," it follows that feeling consists of the twelve links [of dependent origination].
According to Sengliang:
"Feeling is the link of initial consciousness."
Consciousness is able to undergo birth; therefore, it is called "feeling" (*vedanā*).
The *Daohui ji* states:
"One should know that this feeling is itself formative action (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*)."
This future link of consciousness arises from the link of karmic consciousness of the present life and is obtained through the karma of the present life;
therefore, it is itself both *saṃskāra* and *bhava*. This karma is also termed *saṃskāra* and is also termed *bhava*.

Regarding the statement that "from the causal conditions of feeling, name-and-form, ignorance, craving, grasping, becoming, and volitional formations arise," these are all matters pertaining to one's future life.
Following this "name-and-form," there should be the six sense bases, contact, and feeling; however, these three links are omitted here.

Feeling, contact, consciousness, the six sense bases, and so forth—therefore, that which experiences [feeling] is precisely the twelve links. This, moreover, pertains to matters within a subsequent existence.

Because there is ignorance, craving, grasping, becoming, and formations within a future birth, one again gives rise to feeling, contact, consciousness, the six sense bases, and so forth within a subsequent body.
Regarding "the six sense bases and so forth" (*ṣaḍāyatana-ādi*), this is a brief omission of the names of the subsequent links; hence the word "and so forth" (*ādi*).
As for "feeling" (*vedanā*), it is simply the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) at its initial arising.
Regarding "contact-consciousness" (*sparśa-vijñāna*), this refers precisely to the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The four aggregates (*skandha*) are called "name" (*nāman*); the essence of these four aggregates is simply mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika*).
Therefore, when we now speak of "contact-consciousness," this refers to the mind and its factors, which constitute the four aggregates.
Daohui states regarding Tanyan:
"The names of the various factors (*aṅga*) herein, which were previously concealed and not brought forth, are now fully enumerated.
He further says:

Now, although the names for the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) are extremely numerous, if they are categorized as the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), this is a categorization that encompasses the three periods of time.

To distinguish the mental factors across the three periods: from the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) from ignorance (*avidyā*) until its conclusion, there are ignorance, craving, and grasping (*upādāna*). This clarifies that, in the past, there are generally four such factors.

If interpreted according to the twelve links of dependent origination, the first three meanings are collectively subsumed under the link of ignorance (*avidyā*); since craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are components of ignorance, they may be included as a single link.
"One should know that it is 'identical' (ji)" means that the fruit exists without departing from the cause; therefore, they are said to be identical.
Ordinary people do not understand this and claim that they are one and the same entity, lacking the sequential arising of mental factors (citta-caitasika); this is their error.
"From the completion of the experience of birth until further grasping at the formations of existence: this clarifies the mental factors (*caitasika*) of the present.
As for 'experience' (*vedanā*), it refers to the initial consciousness at the moment of birth; therefore, it is designated by the name 'experience.'"
"Action-existence" (*saṃskāra-bhava*) is an alternative designation for "action" (*saṃskāra*) according to its specific meaning.

When understood in terms of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), it is a concise formulation that omits the three links of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and sensation (*vedanā*).

Ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are collectively treated as one member; grasping (*upādāna*) is the member of grasping; and formations (*saṃskāra*) and becoming (*bhava*) are the member of becoming.
As for sensation (*vedanā*), contact (*sparśa*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the members of contact and sensation have been omitted from the list.

If interpreted according to the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), "feeling" (*vedanā*) constitutes the link of birth (*jāti*), while all others are collectively considered links.
Therefore, feeling is that which assists the twelve links.

"Feeling" is the consciousness that undergoes birth in the present; "consciousness" is the master of birth. If one relies upon this master, then all three periods of time possess the twelve [links]. Good son!
When my disciples heard this teaching, they exclaimed, "The Tathāgata says there are no mental factors (caitta).
According to Sengliang:

Upon hearing this teaching, they immediately asserted that there are no mental factors, maintaining that there is only a single mind that functions sequentially, and did not allow for the existence of various factors such as perception (saṃjñā) and feeling (vedanā).
"Good son! In the sutras, I have spoken thus, up to declaring that the Tathāgata says there are mental factors (*caitasika*).
According to Sengliang:..."
Defiled cognition (*akuśala-jñāna*) is the primary condition for consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The reason it is said to be a "condition" is to clarify that within the interval of conditions, when consciousness is obscured, craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*) will necessarily arise.

Regarding "that which arises because of contact": when consciousness abides in its conditions, it is termed "contact" (*sparśa*); thereafter, it is simply termed "consciousness. Their substance is one, though their meanings differ.

However, that which is not contact is obscure when first grasping its conditions, whereas it becomes clear as the various mental factors continue to arise; since their natures differ—being clear or obscure—it is said to be "not [contact].
Those who maintain that there are mental factors (caitta), upon hearing that it is "not contact," assume that the nature of these factors must be distinct.
To claim that [contact] arises simultaneously with [feeling], yet their conditions for grasping differ and they are distinct from the substance of the mind, is to lose the essential meaning.
Sengzong said:

"When I heard it taught that the four dharmas give rise to eye-consciousness, and so on up to the arising of feeling and grasping, I did not understand the sequence; I took them to mean they exist all at once."
This extends even to the twenty-one types of unwholesome minds.
Since neither has ever been experienced, they further give rise to contention. Bao Liang said:

When the initial causal consciousness first arises, it is followed by perception (*saṃjñā*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), and so forth; yet this is not the initial consciousness itself.

People then claim that there is a separate contact (*sparśa*) which can harmonize and give rise to various mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*); since these are not the mind itself, they say "there are mental factors."
According to the Buddha’s intention, one may say that they exist, and one may also say that they do not exist.
Since what precedes is mind and what follows is also mind, there are no separate mental factors (caitta).
Because they take objects as conditions, the various minds come together to collectively condition a single object.
As for the "factors of mind" (*caitasika*), they may also be referred to as "mental factors.

Some people do not understand this; hearing that there are "driving forces" (*cetanā*) which have their own distinct enumeration, and hearing that these [factors] do not exist, they claim it is simply a single mind, arguing that no arising or ceasing can occur within it.
This is why it constitutes a dispute.
The *Dàohuì jì* states:
"That which is designated as 'action' (karma) is called 'action' because of its gravity."
Regarding "contact conditions perception and feeling": this gives rise to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
From pleasant feeling, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) subsequently arises; from craving, various wholesome mental factors (*citta-saṃskāra*) extensively arise thereafter.
That which is produced by contact arises subsequent to the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*).
However, that which is not contact refers to the mental factors such as perception and feeling that arise in succession after consciousness; these are called *caitta* (mental concomitants).
Ordinary people do not understand this and claim that there are separate dharmas of mental factors; this is their error.
"Good son! At times I speak of there being only one *bhava*, up to speaking of five *bhavas*, or even saying there are six *bhavas*.
According to Sengliang:..."
There are sentient beings who possess the five aggregates; these are called the "aggregates of sentient beings" and are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Second refers to cause and effect.
Third refers to the three realms (*tridhātu*).
The fourth refers to the four modes of birth;
the fifth refers to the five destinies;
and the sixth constitutes the six realms of existence.
The seventh refers to the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
The eighth refers to the eight abodes of beings (*aṣṭau devanikāyāḥ*). Some say:
These eight dhyānas do not include the realm of existence (bhava), as they are all essentially like non-humans.
The ninth refers to the nine abodes of sentient beings.
Failing to grasp the Buddha’s intent and failing to understand the relationship between the detailed and abbreviated versions, [the author] simply takes five or six as the fixed number.
Sengzong said: "The fifteenth is the discourse on disputes.
From the Buddha’s teaching of 'one existence' up to twenty-five, all are expedient transformations taught according to the circumstances of various regions."
"Good son! Once in the past, I went to where it was proclaimed: 'One must fully receive the eight precepts of the fast before one obtains them as taught by the Tathāgata.
According to Sengliang: [The text continues].
Regarding "not receiving [the precepts] in their entirety," this means not receiving all five at once.
Because one's mind is weak, one cannot vow to cease the five evils; therefore, the precepts cannot arise.
If one receives all five precepts at once, the mind is strong enough to give rise to them.
If one cannot maintain them in their entirety, one may then relinquish four and retain one; this is called "one part.
It does not contradict the Buddha’s intention to say that receiving only a single precept alone does not constitute full ordination.
Regarding "one obtains it by receiving it in its entirety": this takes one day and one night as the full duration. Why is this?
Because there are two types of lay precepts:
There are two types: lifelong and non-lifelong.

Regarding the non-lifelong type, one sets the duration by the mind; whether for one day, or fifteen days, or one day and night, or merely one month, or even merely one night, it is all sufficient to constitute the observance of the fast (*upoṣadha*).
The Sūtra provides proof:
from the time of Kātyāyanīputra’s inquiry down to the point of a single moment of mindfulness, because that moment of mindfulness is so brief, the mind is unable to give rise to the precepts.
He replied, "It is not accomplished."

Alternatively, some have heard it said that one day and one night constitutes the fixed limit; [if this duration is exceeded or shortened,] the fast is not accomplished in its entirety, which misses the essential point.
Sengzong says: This is the sixteenth point of contention.
If we discuss the correct principle, regarding the five precepts, one obtains their respective blessings according to how many are received and maintained.

However, as for the eight precepts, whether observed for a single day or even for a single moment, they can only be attained if practiced in their entirety; this distinguishes them from the five precepts.
Having heard it said that the five precepts may be received in parts, one might conclude that the eight precepts may likewise be obtained in parts;
having heard it said that the eight precepts must be received in their entirety to be effective, one might conclude that the same applies to the five precepts as well.
Baoliang said:

"Regarding 'one-part upāsakas,' this refers to those whom the Buddha taught at one time that, having already received the three refuges, they receive only one precept from among the five; thus they are called 'one-part' [upāsakas]."
People, failing to understand this, claim that among the five precepts taught by the Buddha, one may receive only a single precept and yet fully obtain all five.
This further gives rise to contentious debate.

Moreover, for the sake of a certain individual, it was said that even a single day and night of virtuous conduct does not constitute attaining the *upavāsa* (fasting/observance); the original statement specified "one day and night," meaning that a mere moment or a single thought does not constitute performing the *upavāsa*.
This person’s goodness is itself the attainment of the precepts.
Some, however, do not understand this and claim that neither the fast nor the precepts are attained; this is why they dispute.
Daohui’s Record states:
Regarding the "one-part upāsaka": this refers to one who has first received the five precepts and subsequently relinquishes four while maintaining one; this is what constitutes the "one part.
If one were to initiate only a single precept from the outset, it would not be possible to generate the unmanifest (avijñapti) karma.
If one says that a lay follower (upāsaka) who leaves home does not obtain [the precepts] because they were not received in their entirety, this misses the essential point.
As for the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), it may be received on the night of the previous day; it is likewise permissible to receive them over two days or even for a single day.

If it is for a single day and night, or for a single thought-moment or a single occasion, these are all called "attaining goodness," but they do not constitute the attainment of the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa).
The Record states:
"As for the fast (zhāi), it consists of not eating after midday."
To remain pure and simple for one day and one night is called *zhāi* (fasting).
The eight precepts are for the purpose of adorning this *zhāi*; therefore, it is termed the "eight-precept *zhāi*.

However, if one receives the eight precepts for only a single thought-moment or a single instant, it is not that they cannot be received; rather, because the *zhāi* is not fully accomplished, one is said to have attained goodness, but it is not called attaining the *zhāi*.
Ordinary people do not understand this and claim that one must receive the eight precepts in their entirety for a full day and night to obtain the method of the Eight Precept Fasting;
this is an error. Good son!
In my sutras I have stated that once one commits a grave transgression, one has already lost the bhikṣu precepts.
According to Sengliang:
It is called "slayer of thieves" because it refers to slaying the thieves of affliction (*kleśa*).
Because pure precepts can give rise to pure wisdom, they are called "the precepts received by the Noble Ones."
Having committed a grave offense, one breaks the noble precepts and is no longer called a bhikṣu.
Regarding the loss of the status of a bhikṣu, upon hearing that the noble precepts one has received are lost, it is said that everything is lost; this refers to the loss of their essential purpose.
Sengzong said: "This is the seventeenth point of contention.
If we discuss the correct principle, one who commits the four grave offenses is one whose [nature] has not been produced; those who have not committed them all remain present."
Daohui said: "It depends on the specific offense committed.
Baoliang’s record states:
It is simply that one cannot give rise to the untainted (anāsrava) ear; it does not mean that the precepts are entirely lost, for there still remains the state of having broken the precepts.
To say that by committing a grave offense one completely loses them and is no longer a bhikṣu is to miss the essential point.
"Good son! In a sutra, I have explained for Cunda that even after committing the four grave offenses, one does not lose the prohibitive precepts.
According to Sengliang:
The "attainment of the Way" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path.
These three are all pure precepts; attaining them without outflows is called "reaching," while worldly non-outflow states are called "receiving," and those not yet reached are called "indicating."
That which defiles the path is contrary to this: purity leads to Nirvana, and thus is called the "path.
That which defiles is impurity and is not the path.
Not losing the prohibitive precepts means that pure precepts are ever-present.
To coexist with evil karma is called "defilement," just as throwing a jade gem into mud is called "defiling the jade"; this misses the essential point.
Sengzong said: "Upon hearing the teaching of non-arising, one immediately says that everything is lost."
Upon hearing it said that one defiles the Path, he immediately claimed that even if one commits a grave offense, the prohibitive precepts are not lost. Baoliang said:
"What is now called 'defiling the Path' means that because one has violated the precepts and defiled one's conduct, one cannot attain the Holy Path."
However, for those who have not attained [realization], even if they hear of a transgression, they lose [the precepts] regardless of whether they actually committed it;
if they hear of defilement, they are all defiled and do not retain [the precepts], regardless of whether they actually committed it.
Therefore, this constitutes a formal debate.

and the seventh uses the analogy of seven types of persons to illustrate cause and effect in general.
The eighth [section] serves as a metaphor for the fruit.
This first [section] clarifies the Middle Way of the internal and external.
Zhi Xiu said:
Kāśyapa has already expressed his conviction, the intent of which is to benefit sentient beings.
From this point onward, the Buddha extensively elucidates the Middle Way. "Good son!"
"For the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain understanding and liberation, I have declared that Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external.
According to Zhixiu’s commentary:
"The following two sections distinguish the Middle Way."
Below this, first, the Middle Way that is neither internal nor external is clarified in order to refute the attachments held by others.
Second, by means of six kinds of causes and conditions—such as space and the horns of a rabbit—the Middle Way that is neither existent nor non-existent is clarified.
Why is this? Ordinary beings may say that the Buddha-nature exists apart from the aggregates (skandhas), being like empty space.
According to Sengliang:
This raises the point of divergent views.
Briefly, there are two types:

Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of the Middle Way; because it reaches [the truth], it is called the Middle Way. This is called the analytical answer.
According to Sengliang:
"Permanence is the nature of the fruit, and impermanence is the nature of the cause; when both natures are impartial, it is called the Middle.
Sengzong said:
The reckoning of ordinary people is logically incorrect.
As for the principle of Buddha-nature, this principle is neither internal nor external; first, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are cited to clarify this meaning.
If one says it exists only internally, both [positions] are improper.

Now, when it is said that the Buddha-nature is provisionally internal, provisionally external, and established through their combined function, this refers to the presence of both the direct cause (正因) and the objective cause (境界因). Since it is not accomplished apart from these, the efficacy of their combined function is taken as the Middle Way.
Regarding the fivefold analysis of the "conjunction of application," this is the first analysis.
Furthermore, son of good family!

According to Sengzong,
the second [section] clarifies the appropriate application by means of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).
Furthermore, "O son of good family!..."
Some say that the Buddha-nature, when it reaches [its fulfillment], is called both internal and external; this is termed the Middle Way.

"The third point concerns the fruit, wherein one should clarify the application of the True and the Responsive."
Furthermore, son of good family!

Fourth, regarding the application of wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) through illumination:
Furthermore, son of good family,
some may say that reaching both the internal and the external is called the Middle Way.

the fifth point briefly demonstrates that practice and realization are mutually inclusive.

Furthermore, son of good family!
Some may say that reaching both the internal and the external is called the Middle Way.
According to Sengzong, it is said:

"The buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither existent nor non-existent," up to "the buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither existent nor non-existent.

Space cannot be seen by people as being permanent, nor can it be seen as definitely existing.

There is a Middle Way within existence, which consists of various forms of emptiness.
While a rabbit’s horn is definitively non-existent for humans, the Buddha-nature is not definitively non-existent for humans; this is the Middle Way within non-existence.
"Neither existent nor non-existent" means it is not the existence of empty space, nor is it the non-existence of a rabbit's horns.
"Also existent" refers to that which is destined to exist;

Sengzong said: "This second point explains the internal and external by means of 'neither existent nor non-existent.
