some say there is no retribution for good or evil; some say there is good and evil but no Path; some say there is a Path but it cannot be attained through cultivation; some say men can attain it while women cannot; some say those who have left the household life can attain it while those who remain at home cannot; and some say those free from desire can attain it while those still possessed of desire cannot—these constitute two [sets of] questions.
Baoliang said:
"There is likewise no fixed dogma.
The reason the Buddha remained silent was that he wished to manifest his own traces; it was not intended as a response of setting aside the question."
The Buddha said:
"Vatsa, excellent, excellent! It is right that the rain of the Dharma falls equally upon both upāsakas and upāsikās."
According to Sengliang:

"Regarding the three types of wholesome and unwholesome, as well as the ten types of wholesome and unwholesome—the three pertain to the supramundane, while the ten encompass both the mundane and the supramundane.
Baoliang said:
The Buddha has now answered that by giving rise to the three wholesome roots and abandoning the ten unwholesome paths, one ultimately severs all obstacles and accomplishes the Noble Path.
"World-Honored One!
If various non-Buddhists wish to come forth from the household life, they shall go to the place where their corpses are and perform great offerings there."
According to Sengliang:

"The 'trial in the fourth month' refers to those of external paths who, holding fundamentally different views, donned robes to steal the Dharma; all such individuals were subjected to this trial in the fourth month.
If they were not of such a nature, there would have been no need for a trial."
Baoliang said:
"As the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states, 'a six-month trial,' this method exists simply because it accords with individual capacities.
As for the case of the Vātsīputrīya who attained the first fruit only after fifteen days had passed, the workings of cause and response differ in each instance; this is what is recorded here."
The *Naiyi* (Naked) Brahmin further stated: "That the body is either virtuous or non-virtuous—this meaning is not so.
According to Sengliang:

"The reason for asserting that there is no cause and effect, thereby establishing the *icchantika*, is because they claim that good and evil possess an inherent nature (*svabhāva*) and do not arise from causes and conditions; it is not that good and evil themselves do not exist."
Baoliang said:
"When one traces the beginning of sentient beings, there is no source; therefore, it is said that both good and evil are all natural. Why is this so?"
As Gautama says that because of afflictions [things] arise, and thus all possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) rather than arising from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
According to Sengliang:
"The first point means that 'before' and 'after' cannot exist simultaneously; by taking the body as an analogy, he asserts that all phenomena are without cause."
Baoliang said: First, I shall pose three challenging questions.
The first concerns the sequence of the afflictions and the raising of the entire body.
Furthermore, Gautama!
Solidity is the nature of earth; because it exists by virtue of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is not produced by causes and conditions.
According to Sengliang’s commentary:
Second, [the text] uses emptiness to categorize the five great elements, and uses the five great elements to categorize all things.
Baoliang says: "The following seven points are raised as evidence for this principle."
This first point proves that each thing possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, Gautama!
Regarding the phenomena of the world, how can you say they arise from causes and conditions?
According to Sengliang:
"The third [point] is that just as wood does not depend on being good or evil, yet its nature possesses the utility of being crooked or straight;
so too the natures of the five destinies possess goodness or evil, receiving their names according to the place of birth."
Baoliang said:
Second, it is proven that because there is a fixed application [of causes], there are no causes and conditions.
Furthermore, Gautama!
"All sentient beings, up to all phenomena, each possess its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
According to Sengliang:
"The fourth [point] holds that when one seeks objects by way of their categories, each possesses its own nature."
Baoliang said:
"This is the third proof.
Furthermore, Gautama!"
As Gautama has said, all phenomena arise from their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
According to Sengliang’s commentary:
Fifth, because the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are not the cause of greed, hatred arises spontaneously.
Baoliang said:
"This is the fourth matter.
Furthermore, Gautama!"
I observe that worldly people each possess their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*) and do not arise from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
According to Sengliang:
"The sixth [point] means that if there were causes, it would be illogical for those who are identical to obtain two different fruits, namely suffering and pleasure."
Baoliang said:
"This is the fifth matter.
Furthermore, Gautama!"
Worldly children [claim] that all phenomena each possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
According to Sengliang,
the seventh [point] refers to the absence of causes for sorrow and joy.
Baoliang said:
This is the sixth matter.
Furthermore, Gautama!
"Worldly dharmas are of two kinds, up to those that possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because they possess intrinsic nature, they do not arise from causes and conditions.
According to Sengliang:
"The eighth [category] refers to the externalist calculations: space has both function and name, whereas a rabbit's horn has neither function nor name."
Baoliang said:
"This is the seventh matter.
All seven matters are simply proofs of spontaneity."
The Buddha said:
"Good son! That which you have described as being identical to the five great elements is impossible."
According to Sengliang,
he first refutes the second [position], clarifying that the great elements are impermanent and therefore lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Baoliang says:
If all phenomena were derived from the five great elements, then since all phenomena are impermanent, the five great elements would likewise have to be impermanent.
Good son! You claim that because the locus of function is fixed, you conclude that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
According to Sengliang,
this is the response to the third point.
If names and meanings have causes, then reality likewise has causes.
Baoliang said: This answers the second point.

It clarifies that when bamboo and wood first grow, they originally lack the nature of being arrows or arrowheads; it is through the work of craftsmen that they are formed—how, then, is this not due to causes and conditions?
"Good son! As for your statement that 'just as a tortoise born on land [attains its limbs], there is neither self-nature nor a single nature,' according to Sengliang’s commentary:"
This is the answer to the fourth point.
It clarifies that if a tortoise lacks the necessary conditions, it may likewise enter fire.
Baoliang said:
Answering the third proof: since all things arise from karma and conduct, how could they possibly be without causes?
Son of good family!
You ask why the body comes first; by what cause and condition do you raise this objection?
According to Sengliang, this is the response to the first objection:
"Your nature is likewise without before or after, and my conditions likewise have no priority or sequence; why, then, do you raise this objection?"
Baoliang said: Having completed the refutation of the three proofs, he answers what his opponent has maintained.
For now, he provides a general negation to clarify that [the opponent's position] should not be subject to further challenge.
"Good son! The bodies and afflictions of all sentient beings, down to their very limits, all arise from causes and conditions and possess no intrinsic nature.
According to Sengliang:
For you, there is a single moment without cause and effect; for me, there is a single moment with cause and effect.

As for the passage beginning "like the wick and the light," if one were to claim there is no cause simply because one does not perceive the cause of the body, then since you likewise do not perceive the cause of a jar, you should not say that clay is the cause of the jar.
Baoliang said: "This is the correct answer.

To say that the body and afflictions exist simultaneously seems not to concern the beginning of sentient beings; it should properly be a statement made when grasping the branch of 'consciousness' within the twelve links of dependent origination."
Now, taking birth as one's substance necessarily requires the simultaneous arising of both craving that moistens karma and craving that moistens birth.
If there were only craving that moistens karma and no craving that moistens birth, then it would not constitute a karmic retribution.

Therefore, although the arising of the link of consciousness (vijñāna) depends upon the moistening of karma, if the moistening that produces rebirth does not further arise, then the retribution will not continue.
At that time, the body and the afflictions (kleśa) may be said to exist simultaneously.
Although they arise simultaneously, the body must nonetheless depend upon afflictions to exist.
If you claim that the body does not precede [the afflictions] and thus knows no cause, this is not so; for we clearly observe that things such as vases do not arise without causes and conditions.
"Good son! If one says that all dharmas reach [the ultimate], one should likewise diligently uphold the precepts.
According to Sengliang:
This means that in your doctrine, that which can produce [something] is called "great"; if there were no causes and conditions, it should not be called "great. Baoliang said:
"The body is preceded by causes and conditions; it is the same in this regard."
"Good son! As for your statement that the five great elements possess a fixed, solid nature because they reach [their destination], and thus one cannot say their self-nature is solidity—
according to Sengliang, it is said:"
"These possess fragrance because fragrance belongs to the earth. Bao Liang said:
"This is a further refutation of the initial proof."
Since that [fire] takes ghee as its ground and at times becomes identical to water, how could it possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
Good son! From white tin, lead, pewter, copper, iron, gold, and silver, up to [other substances], how can you say that they are definitively named the nature of fire?
According to Sengliang, it is said:
"This possesses luminous form; form belongs to fire.
Baoliang said:

Fire is not fixed; when it flows, it has the nature of water; when it moves, it has the nature of wind; when it is hot, it has the nature of fire; and when it is solid, it has the nature of earth—thus, it does not possess a self-nature.
"Good son! The nature of water is called 'flowing. When water freezes, it occurs due to causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions.
According to Sengliang:
Because it possesses the nature of solidity, it is called water.
However, since the nature of movement is common [to both], if something moves without losing its nature of flowing and maintaining itself, would it not be called wind?
If movement is not called wind, and if moisture predominantly belongs to water, then when it is frozen and solidity predominates, it should belong to earth.
How could these names be derived from their conditions?
Baoliang said:
"If that which is frozen still belongs to water, then since waves originally move because of the wind, one ought to name the waves 'wind.
If one does not name the waves 'wind,' then one likewise should not name the frozen state 'water.'"
"Good son! Your statement—that it is impossible for greed to arise from anything other than the five sense objects, up to the point where greed for liberation arises—is not so.
According to Sengliang:
Answering the fifth objection:
"Not the cause" refers to the primary cause.

Regarding the two causes of greed: discursive thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are the internal cause, while the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are the external cause; from the internal, the external arises.
"Good son! As for your statement that the possession of all faculties up to the absence of intrinsic nature all arise from causes and conditions," according to Sengliang:
Answering the sixth objection:

There are those who are generous yet poor, and those who are stingy yet wealthy; this should be addressed by the same objection as that regarding the sense faculties. Therefore, the result of past karma is answered first.
The direct answer is that while the faculties are complete and one possesses great wealth, these conditions are not concurrent during the period of cultivation;
they differ only when the retribution is received. Good son! As you have said, for worldly children, this body arises from the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma.
According to Sengliang’s commentary:
This answers the seventh objection.
If laughter were an inherent nature (*svabhāva*), then one ought to laugh constantly.

Just as fire that ceases its heat would be eternally hot, [the Buddha] did not answer the eighth question regarding space or the horns of a rabbit; these were all set aside as non-answers (*sthāpanīya*).
The Brahmin said:
"World-Honored One!
If this body reaches the point of eliminating the afflictions of the three realms and attaining the fruit of Arhatship.
According to Sengliang:
I further entreat the Buddha to explain the causes of the body; upon hearing it, I shall immediately attain awakening.
Furthermore, there was a Brahmin named Hongguang (Vipula) who was able to give rise to the unsurpassed and vast mind of enlightenment.
According to Sengliang’s account:
"Hongguang has concealed his traces, leading those who are ignorant to respond to the propagation of this sutra.
Now that the time for him to manifest his traces is approaching, what we have heard will not be far off."
Baoliang said:
"He had no further attachments; he simply formed a mental thought to test the Buddha.
The Buddha immediately knew what he was thinking, which surpassed even what his own mind could perceive, and thereupon [the dragon] submitted."
Therefore, when Kauṇḍinya first questioned his own actions, the Buddha immediately revealed his traces.
The Buddha said:
"Stop, stop!"
"Kauṇḍinya, you have now been able to give rise to such a great resolve.
According to Sengliang’s commentary:
"To 'enter' means to enter nirvana; to 'emerge' means to emerge from birth-and-death."
At that time, the World-Honored One, having known this, immediately addressed Kauṇḍinya, asking where the bhikṣu Ānanda was now located.
According to Sengliang’s commentary:

"There are two persons for the circulation of the sutra: those above [Kauṇḍinya] were entrusted with its broad propagation; from Subhadra downward, it should be handed over to Ānanda. The subsequent text seems to imply this.
It may also be explained that while the principle is entrusted to Hongguang, the text is entrusted to Ānanda. Baoliang said:
"From this point downward, the text correctly reveals the intent of the propagation [of the Dharma]."
There are three reasons for inquiring after Ānanda’s whereabouts:
first, to manifest that Ānanda possesses eight inconceivable virtues; second, to ensure the circulation of the sutra; and third, for the sake of Subhadra.
Kauṇḍinya said: "World-Honored One!
The bhikṣu Ānanda has not come to this great assembly."

According to Sengliang, Māra wished to ensure that the Buddha-dharma would have no one to whom it could be entrusted, so that it would be extinguished and not transmitted; for this reason, he disturbed and troubled Ānanda.
Baoliang said:
This was to manifest Ānanda’s virtue: that although he was not present in the assembly, he was nonetheless able to receive and uphold [the teaching].
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī went to inquire after the whereabouts of Kauṇḍinya and Ānanda.
According to Sengliang’s commentary:
It was in order to manifest Ānanda’s virtues that he posed the question.
At that time, from the World-Honored One’s address to Mañjuśrī until the words "if the Buddha permits," it refers to [Ānanda] going to serve as an attendant.
According to Sengliang’s analysis:
Ānanda possesses two qualities; first, he is a kinsman whom people revere and trust;
second, he has received and upheld the Buddha’s words without any error or omission.
Mañjuśrī! Ānanda served me for eight years, fully attaining the wisdom born of hearing.
According to Sengliang:
The introduction concerning Ānanda has three points.
First, it describes his conduct and activities, noting that he possesses eight inconceivable virtues and is thus certainly capable of widely propagating [the Dharma].
Second, it provides scriptural evidence, clarifying that among the disciples of the seven Buddhas, those who possessed these eight virtues were all authorized to circulate [the teachings].
Third, the correct explanation of Mañjuśrī’s question: "Mañjuśrī!
From the attendant of Vipaśyin Buddha down to the bhikṣu Ānanda, they constitute the treasury of great learning."
According to Sengliang, the second [point] cites the Seven Buddhas as an example.
"O son of good family! [he says].
"As you have said, within this great assembly, those who reach Ānanda will be able to hear it themselves and propagate it.
According to Sengliang:
"The third [section] is the direct answer to the question."
"Mañjuśrī! The bhikṣu Ānanda, having paid his respects with the utmost sincerity, withdrew and stood to one side.
According to Bao Liang’s commentary: [The text continues as follows].
As the time [for his passing] was about to arrive, he commanded Mañjuśrī to dispel the māras with a mantra and summoned Ānanda back.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Go from outside this Śāla grove to where Subhadra is, and return to me. [Ānanda] went to where Subhadra was and returned to the Buddha's presence.
According to Sengliang’s commentary:
"Those whose habits (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted have merely suppressed the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm, but have not yet suppressed their habits.
At that time, Subhadra arrived, offered his greetings, and immediately attained *nirvāṇa*; what is the meaning of this?
According to Sengliang:

"A person who is arrogant does not wish to personally suffer humiliation; therefore, they feign adherence to external teachings to clarify that gain and loss lie with the other party, not with themselves."
Baoliang said:

"What Subhadra clings to is that all present suffering and pleasure are entirely the result of the past and do not depend on the present; therefore, he intends to end his suffering by throwing himself from a cliff or leaping into fire."
The Buddha said:
"Good son, because there are śramaṇas who have reached this state, I now reprove you for your past karma."
According to Sengliang’s assessment:
"I fear this is what has been established through the errors of the transmitters.
If that person were to say:
"Gautama! I truly do not know whether it is only past karma that exists and not present karma.
According to Sengliang:
Regarding the question of whether one who experiences minor suffering due to causes and conditions can subsequently experience moderate or superior suffering:
does this mean that [the former] can be transformed into [the latter]? If you say it can be attained, then it is not fixed; how then can you definitively state that past karma has been severed?
Furthermore, one should ask:
"Since this present suffering has already reached the past and been exhausted, how can there still be suffering?
According to Sengliang:
If suffering from the past existed, it should have been exhausted along with its karma and should not be experienced again.
Baoliang said:
"If present ascetic practices can sever past karma, then by what means would these practices of suffering themselves be severed?"
"O Benevolent One!
That such ascetic practices could cause the karma of pleasure to reach this state is not so. Why is this? O Benevolent One.
According to Sengliang:
Next, he asks regarding the karma of the four dhyānas and above, which is without suffering or pleasure and is untainted (*anāsrava*) and without retribution:
"For what reason does one undergo such asceticism (*duṣkara*), given that it can neither destroy nor transform [karma]? Why does one undergo it?
It is like a person who, having eliminated an enemy for a king, subsequently undergoes suffering or pleasure due to past karmic deeds.
According to Sengliang:
this proves the existence of retribution in the present life; it does not necessarily mean that [all] results are caused solely by past karma.
"O Benevolent One!
If, by the power of severing the causes and conditions of karma, the mind is likened to a forest and the body to a tree.
According to Sengliang:
The retribution cannot be fully exhausted; if one were to obstruct it, one would not receive [the fruit].
If suffering were taken as the retribution, then animals should attain the Way.
As for "one must first harmonize the mind": the body is likened to a tree; in a forest, the trees are few while the woods are many.
The four aggregates are likened to a forest, and the aggregate of form is likened to the trees; fear arises from the mind, not from form. Subhadra said:
"World-Honored One!"
"I have already first subdued [myself] to the point of receiving this evil body; how much more so for the rest.
According to Bao Liang’s commentary:
"After the Buddha rebuked him, he was able to eliminate coarse perceptions; why not use blood to eliminate subtle perceptions?"
“World-Honored One!
How can one sever all forms of existence and attain unsurpassed bodhi through the contemplation of supreme wisdom?
According to Sengliang:

There are both provisional emptiness and ultimate emptiness; yet the non-Buddhists suppress their fetters by taking conditioned existence as their object rather than emptiness, for to take emptiness as an object is itself a substantialist conception.
Baoliang said:
"There are only the two truths; to forget [subject-object] characteristics is the substantialist conception, and one truly cuts off afflictions through wisdom."
To form mental conceptions and engage in verbal designations—this is the essential purport [of this teaching].
When this Dharma was being expounded, ten thousand bodhisattvas and [the others] down to Subhadra attained the fruit of arhatship.
According to Baoliang:
Regarding those who attain the realization of "one more birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*), they shall attain Buddhahood immediately after that single lifetime.

If this were merely the retribution for the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*), it could not be reconciled with the notion of one or two lifetimes; rather, it is explained in terms of the manifested response (*nirmāṇa*).
If one were to seek analogies from other sutras, they would remain incomplete; as there is no affinity for this [teaching] in this land, it was established that not all [of the text] has arrived.
